Dokters van de Wereld provides primary care in Gaza and has, in a report, mapped the impact of the war and the Israeli blockade of humanitarian aid. The aid organisation speaks of a genocide. For example, 97 percent of the Palestinian population has been displaced. Nearly half have been moved between five and ten times and one in five even more than ten times, according to the report. For the research, Dokters van de Wereld interviewed 416 widows, pregnant women, women who are breastfeeding and carers of children under 5 years old. Diseases Because of the displacement, Palestinians end up in overcrowded and unsafe shelters without access to, for example, clean drinking water and sanitation. As a result, the population is extremely vulnerable to diseases that spread quickly. According to the report, 84 percent of children under 5 were ill in the three months before the research. They suffered from, among other things, diarrhoea and skin conditions. Among pregnant women this was 57 percent. Nearly all pregnant women and women who were breastfeeding had symptoms of anaemia, according to the report. Attacks on care facilities Access to care is hardly available for Palestinians because the care system has completely collapsed, says Dokters van de Wereld. The organisation says that despite the ceasefire in effect since last October, attacks on the care system continue. Between January and August there were, according to the report, 45 attacks on, among other things, care facilities. In those attacks ten aid workers were killed and dozens of others were injured. Three clinics of the aid organisation were forced to relocate in recent years because of Israeli attacks. The Israeli blockade of medical aid also causes major shortages in care. Combating diseases that are easy to cure is difficult because there is little or no medication. Because of the dire situation, more and more Palestinians need psychosocial care. According to the report, the number of people in need of psychological help has more than doubled in recent years to one million in 2025. According to the aid organisation, that help is hardly available because of the destruction of the care system in Gaza. Dokters van de Wereld sees that structural food insecurity is a source of fear for almost the entire Palestinian population. 84 percent of Palestinians find it very difficult to get nutritious food. Palestinians have become dependent on soup kitchens and communal kitchens run by aid organisations. People skip meals or reduce their portions, for example so they can feed their children, the report says. Food diversity is also low. Israel mainly allows food with a low nutritional value and little protein, says Dokters van de Wereld. As a result, people have a shortage of iron, zinc and essential fatty acids that are found in meat, fish, nuts and seeds. A shortage of calories and nutrients has major consequences for the recovery process and the development of children. This year alone, the aid organisation has treated more than 450 children and 1,500 pregnant women and women who are breastfeeding for malnutrition. Reconstruction Dokters van de Wereld says that the "deliberately created crisis" makes it impossible for Palestinians to recover physically and mentally. The NGO calls on governments to stop the Israeli war violence in Gaza and to ensure that constant emergency aid is permitted, so that Palestinians can recover and rebuild their lives.

title: Drought worsens foundation problems, nearly half a million homes threatened
lead: The autumn weather seems to be truly arriving today, but the extreme drought of recent months will affect the Netherlands for a long time. Building companies that repair foundations also have their hands full. More people are sounding the alarm because after their holiday they discovered cracks in the wall. It is expected that many more homes could suffer damage in the coming years due to foundation problems. Extreme weather conditions caused by climate change can worsen those problems. Soil subsidence expert Otto Levelt of knowledge institute Deltares thinks that people with a house with a shallow foundation on clay soil can expect some damage during this period. "Zo was 2018 erg droog en toen zagen we in die gebieden ook meer problemen ontstaan." Due to drought the clay soil shrinks, and with a shallow foundation that shrinkage can continue to below the house. This can cause cracks in walls, or a window or door can start to stick. Nearly half a million homes: Deltares monitors what is happening in the clay at a few places in the Netherlands, such as in <entity id="org:gemeente-arnhem">Arnhem</entity>. There are some neighbourhoods there with foundation problems. The costs can rise to tens of thousands of euros. In Arnhem and other municipalities counters have been opened to help residents, but prevention is even better, says Levelt. There are also many homes on piles and peat and sand soil that are dealing with subsidence. Deltares calculated together with research institute <entity id="org:zbo-nederlandse-organisatie-voor-toegepast-natuurwetenschappelijk-onderzoek">TNO</entity> that 425,000 homes have foundation problems or can get them within a short time. The Knowledge Centre Foundation Problems Approach (KCAF) expects that this number will rise due to climate change over roughly thirty years to around 687,000 properties. That casts a dark cloud over the housing market. Since 1 April, valuation reports for the sale of a house must contain an indication of the condition of the foundation. Only people often don't know what the real state of their foundation is. The report often remains at that indication, based on the location of the house. Changing climate: "We vinden dat huizen een soort woningpaspoort moeten krijgen", says director Frank van Lier of KCAF. "Daarmee kunnen mensen alles over hun huis te weten komen." He sees that homeowners are burying their heads in the sand when it comes to foundation problems. "Terwijl 30 procent van de huizen met deze problemen te redden zou zijn met preventie." Soil subsidence expert Levelt sees that there is still a lot possible. "Alleen moeten we dan wel klimaatbestendig bouwen." Clay soil can, for example, be covered to prevent drying out. "Ook denken we dat druppelirrigatie rondom het huis kan helpen om het vochtig te houden. Dieper funderen is natuurlijk ook heel belangrijk." Levelt points out that prolonged drought, alternating with heavy showers, is more likely to be expected due to climate change. For all kinds of homes that is a problem. "Een ondiep gefundeerd huis zakt bij een slappe ondergrond steeds dichter naar het grondwater toe." That can lead to moisture problems and mould, or water nuisance when a lot of rain falls. Paying up: If the groundwater level becomes too low, homes on piles can also remain too dry for too long. Then pile rot can occur, which ultimately makes the homes unstable. It is just difficult to influence the groundwater level under your home. In addition, tenants remain dependent on their housing association or private landlord to tackle foundation problems. Politicians must therefore step in, KCAF and Vereniging Eigen Huis think. Vereniging Eigen Huis believes that homeowners should receive support. "Natuurlijk kan de overheid niet altijd de portemonnee trekken, maar de onzekerheid is nu wel erg groot door de kosten die op sommige mensen afkomen", says Simon Vrijsen of the interest group. "Als huiseigenaar heb je geen invloed op de oorzaken en je kunt je er ook niet tegen verzekeren." The <entity id="org:zbo-stichting-autoriteit-financiele-markten">Autoriteit Financiële Markten</entity> earlier calculated what the total costs are if all homes with foundation problems are repaired. That comes down to just over 11 billion euros. Some homeowners can pay this themselves, for example by increasing the mortgage, but around 75,000 of them cannot.

title: Will Trump now get the Nobel Prize? Previously someone who can resist him, experts say
lead: In Norway it will be announced tomorrow who will receive the Nobel Peace Prize this year. That is most likely already decided, but regardless of who the winner is, it will raise eyebrows in the White House. The American president is not expected to receive the peace prize. Last year President Trump declared himself the rightful winner. The Nobel Prize was however awarded to Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado "haar onvermoeibare inzet voor het bevorderen van democratische rechten voor de bevolking van Venezuela". The White House criticised the Nobel Committee for having let "politiek boven vrede" prevail. Trump claimed that he had ended "acht oorlogen" and that therefore only he deserved the prize. Later Machado offered her prize to Trump anyway during a visit to the White House, shortly after the US captured Venezuelan president Maduro. The Nobel Institute responded that a Nobel Prize cannot be withdrawn, shared or passed on to others. War with Iran: This year Trump has been remarkably quiet ahead of the announcement. According to news agency Reuters he has been nominated by Cambodia, Israel and Pakistan. Israeli prime minister Netanyahu nominated Trump last year too. Historian and geopolitical analyst Ivo van de Wijdeven sees no great chance of the peace prize for the American president. "Het bestand tussen Hamas en Israël dat vorig jaar werd onderhandeld heeft weliswaar standgehouden, maar er is nog niet echt vrede", he says. Moreover, Trump himself started the war against Iran at the beginning of this year. "Een van de criteria is dat je vrede moet bevorderen." The winner of the peace prize has also been very controversial several times. For example, American Secretary of State Henry Kissinger (1923-2023) won the prize in 1973 for "het gezamenlijk onderhandelen over een staakt-het-vuren in Vietnam" together with Vietnamese politician Le Duc Tho, who refused the prize. Two committee members resigned and The New York Times called it the Nobel Oorlogsprijs. Kissinger was responsible for heavy bombing in North Vietnam and Laos and in the same year supported the bloody coup in Chili. How is the winner of the Nobel Peace Prize chosen? The winner is chosen by the Norwegian Nobel Committee . Members of it are in turn selected by the Storting (the Norwegian parliament) for a term of six years, and can be re-elected. The committee consists of Norwegian citizens. Winners must be nominated. Worldwide there are tens of thousands of people entitled to nominate, such as university rectors, certain professors, heads of peace research institutes and institutes of international relations, members of parliament, members of the International Criminal Court and former winners of the peace prize. The deadline for nominations is 31 January. Subsequently the five-member Nobel Committee reviews all nominations and makes a selection. That is assessed by independent experts. The committee makes a final decision during the last meeting before the announcement. That is based on four main areas: arms control and disarmament, peace negotiations, democracy and human rights. It is not yet clear who is in contention for the prize this year. Nominations are not announced by the committee; the full list of names is only made public after fifty years. Haakon Gjerloew, acting director of the Peace Research Institute Oslo, tells Reuters that he expects someone will be chosen who can withstand Trump's pressure. As examples he names Pope Leo, the International Criminal Court, the International Court of Justice and Francesca Albanese, the UN special rapporteur for the occupied Palestinian territories. Historian Van de Wijdeven does not see the committee letting Trump's choice influence it. He expects the committee to send a message to focus attention on 'vergeten' conflicts. "Toen de prijs vorig jaar aan Machado werd gegeven, was dat ook een signaal naar mensen over een conflict dat veel mensen vergeten waren. Dat zie je bij de Nobelprijsuitreikingen wel vaker." Van de Wijdeven sees Sudan's Emergency Response Rooms as a possible winner. These are networks built up by local people that provide humanitarian aid in the Sudan war, which is also called the biggest crisis in the world but receives relatively little attention. According to Van de Wijdeven that would be in line with the tradition of the Nobel Committee, which often chooses "onbekenden en onbeminden".

title: Rabbits must make growth in the Rotterdam port possible again
lead: The Rotterdam port must get off the 'stikstofslot' and will receive 50 million euros for this from <entity id="org:kabinet">het kabinet</entity>. Of this, nature restoration must be paid next year, so that construction and other permits can be issued again. The industrial expansion of one of the largest and most modern ports in the world must be saved with, among other things, releasing rabbits into nature areas, combating exotic plants and insects, and limiting the number of cyclists and walkers along the coast. This is stated in the 'Routekaart naar natuurvergunningverlening in de Rotterdamse Haven' by, among others, the national government, the <entity id="org:gemeente-rotterdam">gemeente Rotterdam</entity> and the port company. It is one of the 'gebiedsgerichte plannen' with which <entity id="person:jaimi-van-essen">minister Van Essen</entity> wants to tackle the nitrogen problem. "Alles bij elkaar zorgt het ervoor dat we weer vergunning kunnen gaan verlenen", says Arne Weverling (VVD), deputy of the <entity id="org:provincie-zuid-holland">provincie Zuid-Holland</entity>. "Er zijn bedrijven die wel plannen hebben maar niet eens meer een vergunning durven aanvragen. Wij zeggen: dien je plannen weer in. Kom naar Rotterdam." Meijendel and Westduinpark. It concerns nature restoration in Natura2000 areas. These are Meijendel and Berkheide between <entity id="org:gemeente-s-gravenhage">Den Haag</entity> and <entity id="org:gemeente-katwijk">Katwijk</entity>, the Westduinpark in The Hague, and Wapendal, Solleveld and Kapittelduinen between Den Haag, <entity id="org:gemeente-westland">Westland</entity> and Hoek van Holland, and Voornes Duin on the island of Voorne-<entity id="org:gemeente-putten">Putten</entity>. Drinking water is extracted in part of the areas. The areas are professionally managed, among others by dune water company Dunea. And nitrogen deposition is not necessarily the biggest problem there. Water management and coastal protection, for example, are just as important for maintaining nature. It is therefore relatively easy at these locations to achieve the preservation of biodiversity and other Natura2000 objectives. The plan states that rabbits will be released for a "robuust duin-ecosysteem dat bestand is tegen stikstofdepositie". The dunes must be able to drift, and for that keeping the vegetation in check is necessary. Rabbits do that, but their population has declined sharply due to infectious diseases. What does the Rotterdam port have to do with mainly Hague walking areas?, is the question to alderman Tim Versnel (VVD), who is responsible for the Rotterdam port. "In zo'n klein dichtbevolkt landje heb je bijna altijd met elkaar te maken", he answers. "We zijn een team Nederland met elkaar en we moeten met elkaar zorgen dat we weer vooruitkomen." Cooperation with nature organisations: The Rotterdam port itself must also take measures such as closer cooperation between business and nature organisations, more electrically powered equipment in the port, and ships that emit less. Versnel calls the agreements an important first step. "We willen de duurzaamste en sterkste haven zijn in 2050. Dat lukt nu niet. Het zal nog wel wat voeten in de aarde hebben maar we gaan de goede kant op." The Rotterdam Port Company, the municipality and the province of Zuid-Holland have been sounding the alarm for years about the nitrogen problems that threaten the economic activities in the port area. Precisely greening projects are stalled because no permits can be granted. Economic growth: The port is not only suffering from the nitrogen problem. A third of all sustainable projects have been delayed by capacity problems on the electricity grid. Due to all the delays, the investment climate has deteriorated. The port company has also warned about lack of space given the many projects planned, such as a dedicated terminal for defence and the landing of new wind farms. Construction of a new nuclear power plant has since been scrapped. But the Rotterdam port is still in view for small reactors, the so-called SMR's. Restoring the Natura2000 areas is therefore only the beginning.

title: Freight rates for large crude oil tankers rise to a record level
lead: Freight rates for crude oil tankers have reached a record high. Demand for tankers is strong, but there is a shortage worldwide. That is what research by ING shows. "Because of the ongoing war in Iran and disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, tankers have to travel greater distances", says ING economist Rico Luman. Tankers are therefore at sea longer and can be deployed less often. In addition, oil flows from the Middle East are beginning to pick up again, which leads to the extra demand, Luman explains. Attacks Last week most tankers were attacked since the start of the war against Iran, reports the Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC), which is led by the US. This includes attempted attacks, as well as intimidation, for example with drones flying overhead. Last week the number of ships sailing through the Strait of Hormuz fell to the lowest level in two months. Only seven ships made the crossing. Oil exports from the Strait fell as a result. Under the radar The actual oil flows from the Middle East are not fully visible in the official figures, economist Luman says. Some of it happens under the radar, under protection of the American military. "They make use of shuttle services of tankers that sail through the Strait of Hormuz and then transfer the cargo onto other ships." According to the economist, the dollar also has an effect on the record freight rates. The dollar has started to rise against the euro. "Crude oil is traded in US dollars as standard on the world market, so you now need more euros." Money like water At the beginning of this month, renting one tanker cost an average of 500,000 dollars per day. That is ten times the average of last year. "Earlier peaks, such as in 2022 after the invasion of Ukraine, were above 100,000 dollars. But what we see now, we have never seen before", says economist Luman. According to him, prices on routes from or to the Middle East are even higher. And that also means income for tanker shipping companies. "They are making money like water now." For years little has been invested in crude oil tankers. "Especially during the corona crisis, less was driven and flown", explains economist Luman. Now that demand has risen again, orders are also increasing again. But many ships will not be delivered until 2028 at the earliest. Probably after the current rise has passed. Consumers also have to be patient for a while. Although the oil price has fallen somewhat recently, the petrol and diesel prices remain high. "That is because there is little refining capacity, which has been damaged in the Middle East and also in Russia. On top of that, we are dealing with very high transport costs for tankers. That keeps the fuel price at the pump higher than you would expect", concludes Luman.

title: Tropical storm Isaias grows into first hurricane of the Atlantic season
lead: Tropical storm Isaias has grown into the first hurricane of the Atlantic season in the Gulf of Mexico. The American National Hurricane Center expects the hurricane to make landfall tomorrow evening late or Saturday morning early, although it is still unclear where. The states at greatest risk are Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama and Florida. The warm water of the Gulf of Mexico contributes to the rapid intensification of the hurricane. Until now, the Atlantic hurricane season has been very quiet due to a strong El Niño. The winds that El Niño causes make the formation of tropical storms difficult. Isaias is therefore the first hurricane of the season. Life-threatening The center of the hurricane was observed last evening around 745 kilometers south of Mississippi and moved at 15 kilometers per hour, with speeds around it of 120 kilometers per hour. Together with heavy rainfall, that can cause sudden flooding. For the four southern states on the Gulf coast, the National Hurricane Center has issued a warning for a possible storm surge. Mainly the southern parts of Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama and Florida are at risk. The weather institute speaks of a "life-threatening storm surge". More than thirty million people live in the four states. Power outages and evacuations These residents must follow the advice of the local authorities, according to the American hurricane institute. They must also take into account prolonged power outages and possible evacuations. Heavy wind gusts and intense rainfall are also expected hundreds of kilometers inland.

title: Construction company BAM buys specialist in transport pipelines and heat networks for half a billion
lead: Construction company BAM is taking over A.Hak, a specialist in underground infrastructure. The large Dutch construction company is paying 504 million euros for it. A.Hak is a major player in laying heat networks, installing kilometre-long transport pipelines and bringing energy generated at sea ashore. The company from Geldermalsen does this mainly in the Netherlands, but also in Belgium and the United Kingdom. Last year the company made almost 18 million euros in profit. Strengthening BAM top executive Ruud Joosten calls the takeover a major step in the construction company's growth strategy. According to Joosten it ensures that BAM spreads its work even better across the Netherlands. He also expects much from the growth of the company in the United Kingdom due to the construction of water and energy infrastructure. "We are glad that A.Hak continues to play a central role in the further development of BAM's work in energy and underground infrastructure", says Henk Herremans, CEO of A.Hak. The top executive refers to new opportunities for customers and employees. Around 900 full-time employees work at A. Hak. The company expects all employees will remain urgently needed given the major challenge of the energy transition. A.Hak will continue to operate under its own name. Construction With the takeover, Koninklijke BAM Groep B.V. strengthens its position as the largest construction company in the Netherlands. Last year the company earned well over 7 billion euros in construction orders and saw its profit nearly triple to 211 million euros. The construction sector has faced challenges in recent years, such as nitrogen restrictions, staff shortages and uncertainty about construction projects. Relatively many construction companies stopped after the corona period, but large contractors such as BAM, Heijmans and Dura Vermeer are instead receiving many orders.

title: Saudi Arabia: dead and injured in Houthi attack, launch platform destroyed
lead: Attacks by the Houthis yesterday on airports in Saudi Arabia killed three people and also injured 36 people. According to the Saudi authorities, a Moroccan and an Algerian woman died in an attack on Abha airport, in the south of the country near the border with Yemen. In an attack on Riyadh airport a Sudanese man was killed. In response, the Saudi-led military coalition in Yemen attacked 82 military targets, including a launch platform for ballistic missiles. That platform was used for the attacks on the airports. The Houthis in Yemen claim that they carried out a new attack on the airport of the Saudi capital Riyadh. The group calls on airlines to no longer operate flights in Saudi airspace. Saudi Arabia has not yet confirmed the attack. Fighting in Yemen Two days ago, attacks were also carried out on Saudi airports. Last month the ceasefire between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthis, which came into being in 2022, was broken by an offensive by the Houthis. They gained control in Yemen of the entire area along the Red Sea, including the important strait Bab al-Mandab. From that area, military complexes and oil installations in Saudi Arabia are being attacked. Earlier this week the Yemeni government army launched a counteroffensive. According to the Minister of Information, Bab al-Mandab was recaptured. A Houthi spokesperson told the BBC that the attacks on the airports in Saudi Arabia are a response "to the Saudi aggression against our country, which has experienced no fewer than sixty air and missile attacks in the past 24 hours". Because of the situation in Yemen, around 200,000 Yemenis have fled. The UN migration organization (IOM) called on donor countries yesterday to take action.

title: Trade confrontation looms: 'supercrucial' meeting between EU and China
lead: Beijing is hosting a meeting between the European Union and China today and tomorrow. After months of mounting tensions over mutual trade, European Commissioner for Trade Sefcovic is meeting Chinese Minister of Commerce Wang Wentao there. The European Union wants a solution as soon as possible to an increasingly lopsided trade balance that has now grown to 1 billion euros per day. As a result, European industry and employment are hard hit. Sefcovic calls this meeting "supercrucial". China actually benefits from the status quo, because it earns a lot from European consumers. An increasing part of Chinese economic growth must come from exports, because the economy at home is faltering. Fiercer tone The tone of the European Union has become increasingly fierce in recent months. In her annual speech to the European Parliament, Commission President Von der Leyen stressed that the EU-China dialogue must produce concrete results. Otherwise the EU will "use all means at its disposal to restore balance to the relationship". The EU accuses China of unfair trade practices, such as state aid and keeping the Chinese currency artificially low. European companies cannot compete against that. If this meeting yields insufficient results in the EU's view, trade measures may follow. These could consist of duties or even restrictions on imports of Chinese products. No need to meet halfway In China there is little sympathy for European concerns. China points to the strength of its own industry: efficient supply chains, modern factories and cheap logistics, whereby parcels quickly reach customers in Europe. But that is only part of the story. Across the board, European companies do not get the same access to the Chinese market as Chinese companies in Europe. Chinese companies can also easily obtain cheap loans or subsidies, and the Chinese government helps them with free land or business premises. China does not intend to meet the EU halfway. Beijing sees the EU as a weak and divided player and thinks it can make as few concessions as possible by playing member states off against each other. That is a strategy China uses more often. When the European Commission wanted to impose duties on Chinese electric cars last year, China responded with duties on French cognac. In this way China pressured France not to cooperate with the duties on electric cars. If the EU comes with measures in these weeks, China will undoubtedly also respond with a counterattack. The European approach The EU hopes to reach agreements with China on limiting exports to Europe, for example of hybrid cars. The EU also wants better access to the Chinese market for European producers. If China is not willing to conclude a trade deal, extra import duties will be imposed in sectors where Chinese dominance is too great, the EU threatens. In addition, Germany and France, the most powerful countries in the EU, have devised a more far-reaching instrument. This should make it possible to deny China access to the EU internal market more quickly than now. That Germany is also lining up behind this is telling. The country was always cautious in tackling China, out of fear that German industry would be hit by Chinese countermeasures. Focus next week Next week Commissioner Sefcovic will present the results of his meeting to the EU heads of government, when they are in Brussels for an EU summit. Then it must become clear whether the EU is indeed willing to take tough measures, even if those will hurt in Europe because prices rise as a result. Experts urge that those measures be taken, because the economic consequences of doing nothing are greater. In the coming weeks it must become clear whether the EU follows the advice, or whether China is right after all and the EU remains too divided to take firm action.

title: More room for negotiation for buyers, but housing market still tight
lead: Although there is more room for home buyers to negotiate, the shortage on the housing market persists. That is the conclusion of the estate agents' association NVM. Last quarter, affiliated estate agents sold 41,700 existing homes, roughly the same number as a year ago. Because of the summer holidays, there are always fewer transactions in the third quarter. This quarter the decline was larger than usual. An existing home cost an average of 503,000 euros. Prices are rising by almost 2 percent per year. "The market remains tight: almost two thirds of sales are still overbid," says Lana Goutsmits-Gerssen, chair of the NVM. Larger supply comes at the expense of rent. Last quarter, NVM estate agents put 48,500 homes on the market, 5 percent more than a year earlier. The growth is mainly in apartments, where former rental homes came up for sale. "More supply gives home buyers a bit more breathing room," says Goutsmits-Gerssen. "They can more often schedule a second viewing and get more room to negotiate on some homes." At the same time, supply for renters shrank. New-build homes hard to sell. The supply of new-build homes rose 17 percent compared with a year earlier. As a result, supply of new homes is close to the highest level in more than ten years. The higher supply did not translate into more homes sold. The NVM reports that affiliated estate agents actually sold 400 fewer homes this quarter than a year earlier. "Long construction times and high bridging costs make the step harder," says Goutsmits-Gerssen. "Homes need to match what people are looking for and can afford." The average price of a new-build home has also passed the half-million mark since the beginning of 2026. Since then the price has remained roughly the same. Because the price per square metre does keep rising, shrinkflation occurs: for the same price, the buyer gets less living space.

title: Removed wombs and testicles: 'old transgender law caused deep human suffering'
lead: The Dutch <entity id="org:regering">regering</entity> already apologised in 2021 for the transgender law that was in force between 1985 and 2014. Now the research report An Inhumane Law , carried out by researchers from Radboud University, shows how deep the suffering was for the people who had to deal with the law. The researchers, who went to work on commission from the ministry of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-onderwijs-cultuur-en-wetenschap">Onderwijs, Cultuur en Wetenschap</entity>, interviewed 28 transgender and intersex people who paint a picture of the physical, psychological and social harm they suffered because of the law. The transgender law included the rules people had to meet before they were allowed to change their registered sex. Removing testicles and uterus So they first had to be made irreversibly infertile, meaning the uterus and ovaries or the testicles had to be removed, and they had to be unmarried, meaning some felt forced to divorce. A declaration from a doctor and psychologist also had to be submitted. Marloes Hülsken, researcher at Radboud University and one of the authors of the report, says that all this has left deep scars, especially the requirement of irreversible infertility. Hülsken: "Interviewees spoke about the enormous impact this had on their lives: it touched on the wish for children and biological parenthood, forced operations and stopped the production of the body's own hormones. For some affected people this immediately caused a feeling of grief and pain, for others the realisation of the impact only came years later." 'As if I was a criminal' Because of the barriers raised to changing the registered gender, people often lived for many years with incorrect official documents. According to the researchers, this had major consequences for people in daily life. The report cites Carlo Weide. He tells how a pistol was pointed at him at an airport in Greece during a search. "As if I was a criminal, just because my photo matched my face, but what was in my passport did not, the V." Ron de Vries describes his experience: "What affected me most was that everyone thought it was fine to sterilize a young person, because that person may not have offspring. And if you say something about it, then you are the one who is not normal." Man or woman was determined Also the researchers write that people who were born without the medically customary definition of man or woman, and for whom it was determined whether they were a man or a woman, later in life fell under the transgender law for a gender change. "And thereby under the same far-reaching requirements." The government apologised in 2021, after which it was promised that additional research would follow. "This research gives a voice to the transgender and intersex people who were affected by the old law", said <entity id="person:judith-tielen">staatssecretaris Tielen</entity> of Education, Culture and Science. "Their stories show how much pain they have experienced."

title: RTL: chaos at alimony organisation, employees speak of culture of fear
lead: Things are not going well at the government agency <entity id="org:zbo-landelijk-bureau-inning-onderhoudsbijdragen">LBIO</entity>, an organisation that helps people with mediation for child and partner maintenance. RTL Nieuws writes this after its own investigation. Employees of the LBIO speak of a socially unsafe work atmosphere and a "culture of fear", causing more and more people to report sick. As a result, the waiting time to help parents is increasing. State Secretary <entity id="person:claudia-van-bruggen">Claudia van Bruggen</entity> of Justice acknowledges the problems. She sent a letter to <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity> last night. It also states that the Labour Inspectorate has started an investigation. According to RTL, the letter to parliament was sent after the news broadcaster asked the ministry questions about the chaotic situation within the company. The Landelijk Bureau Inning Onderhoudsbijdragen (LBIO) mediates free of charge when an ex-partner pays no or too little maintenance. In 2024, mediation succeeded in 75 percent of requests, so that extra costs and further escalation were avoided. That year the company helped around six thousand people, according to the annual report. 47 percent sickness absence RTL Nieuws spoke with eleven current and former employees. The problems were said to be concentrated mainly in the intervention team, which deals with getting overdue maintenance started. Sickness absence in the department is 47 percent, according to absence figures RTL has seen. On its website the LBIO reports that there are longer waiting times than usual, which can last weeks. An employee who has been there longer calls the waiting times "extreme". Employees paint a picture of people who raise the alarm sometimes urgently needing help to pay their bills and getting into trouble because of the waiting times. "Parents who ask us for help and perhaps have no money to buy food for their children, I get such a stomach ache from it", RTL quotes an employee as saying. Several employees sent a distress letter to the Ministry of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-justitie-en-veiligheid">Justitie en Veiligheid</entity> last summer to make their concerns known. The letter is in RTL's possession. The employees write about the high workload, the backlogs and the sickness absence. A culture of fear is also described. "We are sending this letter anonymously and by post, because we do not feel safe making our name known. (...) Colleagues feel ignored, excluded, intimidated and no longer dare to speak out", the letter states. Jacobine Geel The distress letter also contains strong accusations against interim director Jacobine Geel. The problems are said to have increased since her arrival. They also state that Geel "addressed the team with the high sickness absence in a harsh and intimidating way". At a meeting on 2 July Geel is said to have stated that "the sick must return quickly or go looking for a new job". The employees ask in the letter, which was sent on 8 July, for a new director. RTL Nieuws has audio recordings of closed staff meetings. On them, according to the broadcaster, Geel can be heard calling the workload in the intervention department "skyrocketing". She is also said to have said that the amount of overdue work is "actually no longer manageable" and that action is being taken to "get the situation back under control and calm it down". The LBIO and Jacobine Geel have so far not responded to RTL's questions, the broadcaster writes. <entity id="org:zbo-college-voor-de-rechten-van-de-mens">College voor de Rechten van de Mens</entity> Geel previously got into trouble as chair of the College voor de Rechten van de Mens. In 2024 an independent committee investigated reports about her functioning and found "a pattern of systematically ignoring and excluding". Geel also showed "little sensitivity, empathy and understanding" toward two of the reporters. A pattern of discrimination was not found.

title: Israeli army continues to destroy Gaza, many missing bodies will never be found
lead: "The graves are finished, but still empty", says 60-year-old Mohammed, who hopes that one day he can retrieve his family members from under the rubble. In an Israeli bombing he lost his wife, children, grandchildren and other family members. He has been able to bury some of them, others cannot be found. Still many thousands of Palestinians are missing. More than three years ago, after the Hamas attacks, Israel began a devastating war in Gaza and bombed so intensely that tens of thousands of people ended up under the rubble. It is estimated that more than ten thousand people are missing, a large part of them lying under bombed buildings. Every day relatives and rescue workers, with the few resources they have, try to retrieve remains from the rubble so they can bury them. The victims can sometimes still be recognised by personal belongings such as jewellery, clothing or an ID card. They are buried during large funerals, often dozens at a time. These take place weekly in Gaza. Erased traces But many bodies will never be found, because they lie in areas Palestinians and aid workers are not allowed to enter. Israeli soldiers occupy at least 65 percent of the territory in Gaza. The government of Prime Minister Netanyahu keeps pushing that boundary further, so that the nearly two million Palestinians must survive crowded on the coast in tent camps and destroyed buildings. Palestinians who cross the border markings, or who according to the army come too close, are shot. Satellite images show that behind the so-called 'yellow line' the army is destroying buildings and clearing and moving rubble, while many bodies may still lie in those buildings. The rubble makes way for swept clean plains and military roads and bases. This is shown, among other things, by the analysis of the British research collective Forensic Architecture, which calls its research 'the cartography of genocide'. Using detailed maps, they map the destruction of houses, farmland, hospitals, markets and other infrastructure. Everything Palestinians need to survive as a people. This also erases traces of possible war crimes, the UN warned last month. The UN has long called on Israel to let investigators into the area. And the International Court of Justice has demanded this in the ongoing genocide case. But the border remains closed. Still, investigators can also gather evidence from a distance of destruction and attacks on civilians, using satellite images, videos and witness statements, among other things. Even after last year's ceasefire, which is frequently violated, the army continues to destroy infrastructure. According to the Israeli government this is necessary for its own security. Experts point out that the government is aiming to make the area uninhabitable and to drive out Palestinians. Giving loss a place Exactly where the bodies still lie under the rubble is not known. Only surviving relatives can point out the locations. Moreover, it is difficult to retrieve remains from under the buildings. Israel refuses to let heavy equipment, such as excavators, in. Many bodies have by now largely decomposed. Once the rubble has been cleared, evidence may be lost that can never be recovered, says Jessica Dorsey, who conducts legal research into modern warfare at Utrecht University. "Think of impact traces, fragments of ammunition and the precise physical context of an attack. A case is not made impossible by this, other evidence can reconstruct a great deal." Apart from the research into war crimes, it is very important for relatives that they find and identify their dead, in order to mourn and give it a place. "Recognition of the dead is very important in war situations", says Dorsey. "The disappearance of physical traces can permanently remove that possibility for families." Like many others in Gaza, Mohammed may never be able to bury part of his family. Rescue workers have told him they did everything to find the bodies of his family members, but they have not succeeded. "I so much wanted them to have a grave", says Mohammed. "Then I could visit them on holidays."

title: Gathering ban in Liège after education protests get out of hand
lead: In Liège a gathering ban took effect this morning after education protests got out of hand. It is not permitted to walk on the street with more than three people. In Belgium protests were held in recent days against planned cuts to education. In Liège dozens of activists on Tuesday went past secondary schools, where they smashed windows and set fire to rubbish bins. Police broke up the group. Some shops closed early because of the unrest. There was also vandalism and looting, writes Flemish broadcaster VRT NWS. Violence increases The head of police in Liège speaks of "a continuing increase in violence". He also sees more rioters in the city. According to him, these are people who have nothing to do with the pupils. Yesterday more than fifty people were arrested and several police officers were injured. The gathering ban applies until 6 October at 23.00, says mayor Demeyer. There are exceptions for families, police officers and emergency services. Elsewhere in Belgium it is also restless, but in Liège the protests are the most intense. Call for calm The unrest is, according to minister Quintin of Security and <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-biza">Binnenlandse Zaken</entity>, being stirred up by the Antifa movement. That is an umbrella term for radical left-wing activists who seek confrontation with the far right. "We know that a movement, Antifa-type, is at work in Liège," says the minister. "Adults who manipulate children to convey violent political messages. That is completely unacceptable." Spilled over from France The protests have partly spilled over from France, where since late last month pupils have been demonstrating against deferred maintenance of buildings, classes that are too large and the teacher shortage. Here too it regularly turns into violence. Yesterday police in Marseille again deployed tear gas. According to pupils, police also used stun grenades, which can briefly blind people. The police deny this. A pupil lost his hand this week when a stun grenade exploded in it, after which police announced they would temporarily stop using these grenades.

title: Trial against Dave De K. begins, who killed a toddler and left him on a Zeeland island
lead: The trial against Dave De K. (39) and his ex-girlfriend Romy W. over the death of toddler Dean began today in Ghent. Four years ago, four-year-old Dean was found dead near the work island Neeltje Jans in Zeeland. Belgian De K. is suspected of abduction and manslaughter of the Belgian toddler, and his girlfriend of complicity in the abduction, writes Omroep Zeeland. Dean Verberckmoes's mother voluntarily had herself treated for depression at the time in the psychiatric ward of the hospital in Sint-Niklaas, near Antwerp. She had agreed with De K. and his girlfriend that they would look after Dean. Drank too much During that sleepover things went wrong. W. was in treatment for her alcohol addiction. Because she had nevertheless drunk too much, the couple argued. De K. reportedly drove off angrily with Dean. When the mother wanted to pick up her son a few days later, that was not possible, the couple said. A day later the mother alerted the police. A few days later they tracked De K. down. The toddler was not with him. After a day of police interrogations De K. admitted he had left Dean at Neeltje Jans. In 2010 De K. had already received a ten-year prison sentence for the fatal abuse of his 2-year-old stepson. He served that sentence. Jury The trial is expected to last eight days. A jury of twelve citizens will, together with judges, consider the question of guilt. In Belgium, citizens between 28 and 65 years old are selected for a jury by lot. Today the text is read out stating who is accused of what.

title: At least thirty dead in Russian attacks on city near front line
lead: Russian attacks on the eastern Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk have killed thirty people. That is what the local governor reports. The city lies just behind the front line in the Donetsk region. The Russian army wants to take control of that area. Bombs fell on a street where two city buses were driving. President Zelensky speaks of an attack on a bus stop. Eighteen people were also injured. Governor Vadym Filashkin shared images of rubble in the street on Telegram. A burnt-out bus can also be seen in them. "These are people who were killed by the Russian army", he said. "There is no justification for this, and there can be none." The governor calls on people in the Donetsk region to flee to safer areas of Ukraine. Many civilians refuse to leave their homes and belongings behind. Ukraine has also carried out new attacks on Russia. The army reports that Ukrainian forces have hit the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat oil refinery in the Russian region of Bashkortostan. Death toll in Pryloeky rises. Yesterday there were large-scale attacks at various locations in Ukraine, including the northern city of Pryloeky. Rescue workers found two more bodies there while searching through the rubble. This brings the death toll from the attacks to 22, including five children.

title: The Hague agrees after protracted feud, Van Gogh Museum can proceed with renovation
lead: The ministry of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-onderwijs-cultuur-en-wetenschap">Onderwijs, Cultuur en Wetenschap</entity> (OCW) and the Van Gogh Museum have reached an agreement on the financing of the renovation of the building. "This has removed the long-standing uncertainty about the future of the museum", the museum writes in a press release. According to the Amsterdam museum, a thorough renovation is needed. The building is said to be in poor condition after fifty years of "intensive" use. It is also said to fall short in "the area of safety, climate control and sustainability", as can be read. OCW and the museum could not, however, agree on the financing of the project. The renovation would cost around 104 million euros. And that could not be paid for with the annual subsidy of 8.5 million euros, museum director Emilie Gordenker said last year. At the time, the ministry said the museum was already receiving enough subsidy. Feelings ran high. Gordenker even told The New York Times that the museum might have to close if the state no longer made money available. For a brief moment it seemed the two parties would fight out the financing issue in court, but at the last moment it was decided to talk to each other through a mediation process. Renovation to start in 2028. So OCW and the museum have now nevertheless reached an agreement. What the details of the agreement are is not known. Museum director Gordenker is pleased with the arrangements made: "The renovation is necessary to preserve this building and this world-famous collection in a responsible way for visitors, staff and the generations after us." The renovation will start in autumn 2028. The museum says that the building will not undergo "major changes" and that a large part of the improvements will take place behind the scenes. During the work the museum will be partially open. The permanent collection remains accessible, according to the Van Gogh Museum. It is unclear how long the renovation will take.

title: Maastricht to create 30 elderly zones, against overburdened care and loneliness
lead: Due to ageing, in 2030 one in four residents of South Limburg will be 65 or older. To be able to care for them, existing neighbourhoods in the Maastricht-Heuvelland area are being transformed into a kind of elderly campus. In this way, older people can continue to live independently for longer. In total, 30 so-called living-care zones will be created in the Maastricht-Heuvelland area. This involves an investment of 33.4 million euros, L1 Nieuws reports. That amount is made available by health insurers CZ and VGZ through the Integrated Healthcare Agreement (IZA). The main aim of IZA is to keep healthcare in the Netherlands good, accessible and affordable. From GP to housing transition broker. What the Limburg project makes unique, according to Petra Lamberts, chair of Deltaplan Maastricht Heuvelland, is that care and welfare organisations work together with housing corporations. For example, apartment complexes, mostly social rentals, are being adapted for rollators or wheelchairs and for people with dementia. The entrance or gallery is made more accessible, for example, or a passage to the meeting room is added. To combat loneliness, more activities are organised, for example in a shared living room. Because "loneliness is a predictor of care demand", says Lamberts. "People feel ailments sooner when they are alone. When they take part in activities, they are distracted and people are also stimulated to use their skills." Furthermore, care such as the dentist, outpatient clinic and GP are within walking distance. And the tasks of informal carers can be taken over from time to time, so that they do not become overburdened. Older people who do not yet have a suitable home can ask a housing transition broker to help them search for a suitable senior residence. This is good for housing market mobility, but according to Lamberts it can also relieve care. "We know that if people stay in an unsuitable home for too long, they are more likely to move to a nursing home. Such a move is often disruptive for those people. In many cases they quickly deteriorate." On time. According to Lamberts, this project is not only intended for today's older people, but also focuses on people who will reach old age in the future. "The biggest cost item in care is staff. A year of home care, such as wound care at home or helping people with showering, costs around 12,000 euros per year. But a year living in a nursing home costs more than a hundred thousand." With the 30 living-care zones, she hopes that the limited care staff that is still available can be deployed better. At the moment, nineteen zones are already under development. Next year all 30 must be ready. The plan is ambitious, but badly needed, says Lamberts. "I think there will be no more care collapse, purely because we started on time." She says that the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport sees this project as an example. "This delta plan could well be rolled out across the entire country."

title: In Limburg no dike reinforcement but piles under the house against the rising water
lead: A house in the North Limburg village of Well has been lifted more than one and a half metres and placed on piles. This is meant to provide protection against high water from the Maas and serves as an alternative to traditional dike reinforcement. In total three houses in Well are being placed on piles. The old dike at De Kamp near Well no longer met the latest high water standards, so there was a risk of flooding when the river rose. That happened before in the past. Then the houses flooded. Village character A traditional dike raising would, according to <entity id="org:waterschap-limburg">Waterschap Limburg</entity>, seriously damage the historic village character and the landscape, reports L1 Nieuws. Therefore the Waterschap, for the first time in its history, chose to raise the houses. There was also a financial motive, a representative of Waterschap Limburg explains: "This saves about half the costs compared with a green dike ( red, dike reinforcement )." In total three homes are being raised by about one and a half metres. No wet feet Yesterday, interested people could admire the house on piles from a specially set up viewing point. "I think it is great, it is truly a once in a lifetime chance to see something like this", beams one of the spectators. Another visitor points to the practical purpose of the intervention: "It is remarkable that something like this is possible, but the most important thing of course is that those people will no longer get wet feet." Watch here how it went:

title: Yesilgöz now calls Russia 'the enemy' but that does not mean 'a sudden different approach'
lead: Defence Minister Yesilgöz (VVD) no longer speaks of Russia as "the aggressor" but as "the enemy". With a growing number of sabotage practices, drone attacks and other types of threats and incidents on our continent, the minister believes you have to clearly name what is going on. Such wording about Russia has not been used for a long time, so her words - during the debate on the defence budget in <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity> - caused a stir in The Hague today. Yet for actual policy it means nothing, Yesilgöz explained to the NOS during a suspension of the debate. The policy to invest more in our security, to be alert and to work together with European countries has been underway for years, since the invasion of Ukraine. "It is very clear that Russia is presenting itself as the enemy. That does not yet mean that we are at war or that we will suddenly have a completely different approach." This is how Yesilgöz put it in the Tweede Kamer: the minister does speak of a "new reality" due to the growing number of incidents. Russia was already the biggest threat on our continent, but that threat has grown even larger, she says. The attacks just across the borders of European countries, pinpricks and intimidation have increased recently, the minister says. "Putin is testing how strong our alliance is". Experts advised the minister to name things as they are. "That is what I am doing", said Yesilgöz. <entity id="person:tom-berendsen">Minister Berendsen</entity> of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-buitenlandse-zaken">Buitenlandse Zaken</entity> was asked in a different debate for his opinion on his colleague's statements. In a <entity id="org:kabinet">kabinet</entity> government ministers are expected to "speak with one voice", which means they put forward the same opinion publicly. "The <entity id="pos:minister-van-defensie">minister van Defensie</entity> also speaks on my behalf", said Berendsen. "Russia is our biggest security threat." Berendsen did acknowledge, after various questions from opposition parties, that Yesilgöz had not informed him in advance about her chosen words. Threat assessment Earlier this year the intelligence service <entity id="org:directoraat-generaal-algemene-inlichtingen-en-veiligheidsdienst">AIVD</entity> concluded in its annual report that in eighty years there had never before been a threat picture like the current one. The military intelligence and security service <entity id="org:militaire-inlichtingen-en-veiligheidsdienst">MIVD</entity> also warned in its annual report that the armies of China and Russia are becoming stronger and cooperating more. The House and the minister are debating today the planned multi-billion investments in defence. According to Yesilgöz, the response to threats is being coordinated more and more closely with European countries, but in "essence" nothing changes in the approach. "We were already not naive and we are not going to become so." Embassy angry The Russian embassy in our country is taking the matter seriously. "With her statements, Minister Yesilgöz once again shows that the Netherlands is choosing the destructive route of confrontation", the embassy writes on social media. Russia wants to know whether the minister spoke on behalf of the entire Dutch <entity id="org:regering">regering</entity>. "Russia has no aggressive intentions towards Europe, nor towards the Netherlands", the embassy states. "But at the same time we will not accept threats or ultimatums. We will respond to those directly and crushingly", said the statement.

title: Former head of German intelligence may have passed information on to China
lead: The former head of the German intelligence service has reportedly passed secret information on to China, according to Der Spiegel. According to het nieuwsblad, police are investigating the contacts that former chief August Hanning maintained with Chinese intelligence services after his retirement. Hanning allegedly passed the secret information on to a foreign intelligence service in 2022. To do so, he may first have bought the information from an employee of the Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND), the German intelligence service. According to the police investigation, the employee is said to have shared confidential documents with Hanning for years, including after the former top official's retirement. Hanning (80) headed the BND from 1998 to 2005. He then worked as a private adviser. He is said to have shared the information for payment. Treason: German authorities got onto the case after a house search at Hanning's home, in connection with a kidnapping case. Hanning may have been involved in that, although he denies it himself. During the house search, agents discovered highly sensitive information originating from the BND. It concerned recent documents that the former top official should never have had. The former head of the intelligence service was arrested at his home two days ago. Hanning is suspected of espionage, obtaining state secrets and treason. The former employee who allegedly passed on the information has also been arrested; he was still working for the BND until spring and held a senior position within the service. Activities approved: Der Spiegel also reports today that the BND had officially approved the suspect employee carrying out work for Hanning alongside his work for the intelligence service. Der Spiegel calls it "unlikely" that the disclosure of secrets is legally covered by his secondary position. In this regard, the magazine refers to the German Federal Civil Servants Act, which includes the duty of confidentiality for civil servants.

title: Police hand out dozens of fines for filming accident on A58 near Oirschot
lead: Police fined 29 drivers yesterday for filming a serious accident on the A58 near Oirschot while they were behind the wheel. The Oost-Brabant traffic police wrote on Instagram that taking photos and videos "exceeds every standard of decency". Many emergency services attended the accident yesterday afternoon. They gave first aid to two injured people. An investigation was also carried out. The road was closed in the direction of Eindhoven for several hours. "By filming while in a traffic jam, these drivers apparently accept the risk of a new collision", the police write. "The fine of 449 euros, including administrative costs, apparently does not deter sufficiently." The police say that letters are on their way to the drivers. The police also ask road users to show respect for victims of an accident. "Behind every incident lies a personal tragedy."

title: How neighbours in Rotterdam managed to prevent houses from collapsing
lead: When there are problems with the foundations of your house, it is easier to bury your head in the sand than to tackle the defects, recognises Remco Bruinsma from Rotterdam, who once experienced this himself. "But if your house may be about to collapse, then you really should have an investigation carried out." Nearly half a million homes in the Netherlands have foundation problems or will have them in the short term. Prevention can save many homes, but people often do not know how their home's foundation is doing. "The foundation is actually a kind of silent killer", says Bruinsma. "You don't notice that something is wrong until it is too late." The neighbourhood where Bruinsma lives, the Kleiwegkwartier, was rudely awakened just before King's Day in 2014, he says. "An entire block of houses on the Margrietstraat was evacuated because they had become unsafe. That is so close by that we wondered: what about ours?" Groundwater level A group of residents had research done and, according to Bruinsma, two thirds received bad news. In many places wood rot has damaged the wooden foundations. That can happen when the wooden piles stand dry for too long. Some houses were given another five to ten years, while for other houses the researchers said residents could expect damage from the foundation within five years. Marianna Feenstra also lives in the Kleiwegkwartier and was shocked by the news. She and her husband Jelle were told that their house could last another five to ten years with the current foundation. "My husband wanted to measure the groundwater level himself. So he walked through the neighbourhood with a measuring tape and saw that it was too low everywhere." Together with neighbours, Jelle Feenstra then came up with a plan. To drain rainwater better, the municipality had previously installed a new infiltration system in the neighbourhood. "Jelle often walked past the workers who were laying it and would bring them a cup of coffee", says his wife. "Eventually he asked whether they could install a pump to keep the groundwater level higher, so that not all rainwater is drained away immediately when the groundwater is already low." Pumps After many discussions with the municipality, it succeeded in 2018 in installing such a pump as a trial. "It doesn't raise the groundwater, and the drainage system still works well", emphasises Bruinsma, who was involved in the project. The trial was successful and the pump was eventually added to Rotterdam's pumping stations. The <entity id="org:zbo-stichting-autoriteit-financiele-markten">Autoriteit Financiële Markten</entity> previously calculated the total cost if all homes with foundation problems were repaired. That comes to just over 11 billion euros. Bruinsma thinks that more people in the Netherlands should therefore use a pump to keep the groundwater level up. Soil subsidence expert Otto Levelt of Deltares considers it a clever system that can keep working for quite a long time. "In some areas it is easier than in others, though." Good news At the beginning of this year the Feenstras had their foundation re-examined. A few months later Marianna received the good news: the foundation has been declared sound for the next 25 years. That is the longest period such an investigation can grant. "The groundwater level must of course remain in order in the meantime", says Feenstra. Her husband Jelle did not live to see the news. He died in February. "It's a pity he could not see the good result", says Marianna. She expects that another extra pump will soon be installed in the Statenlaan neighbourhood. "And the pumps are going to be called Jelle 1 and Jelle 2."

title: Podcast De Dag: Jane Doe and the uprising against elite university Cornell
lead: I am Jane Doe. Her name can be seen on signs at Cornell University in the state of New York, on campuses across the US and on social media. The case about the student who was allegedly drugged two years ago by a group of fellow students and then raped stirs up a lot. Listen here: You can listen to this episode of De Dag via NPO Luister and all other podcast apps. Enjoying it? Then don't forget to subscribe. Reporter Simone Tukker tells from the US what is now known about the case. It sparks a discussion about the culture on American campuses and the power of universities and student associations. And online thousands of women are opening the conversation about their experiences. Reactions? Email to dedag@nos.nl Presentation & editing: Marco Geijtenbeek Editorial: Rosanne Sies

title: Rhine water level can no longer be measured: sign switched off
lead: Not far from the point where the Rhine enters the Netherlands, you can normally easily see how high the water in the river is. At the well-known measuring point near Lobith, a large sign with illuminated numbers shows the current water levels all year round. That sign has now stopped working because of the extremely low water levels. The measuring tube attached to the building next to the sign should lie below the water surface in order to take measurements. After months of low water levels, that is no longer the case, so the data is no longer accurate. <entity id="org:rijkswaterstaat">Rijkswaterstaat</entity> has therefore decided to switch off the sign until the Rhine has recovered somewhat. The current water levels can still be followed online. This is done using, among other things, a measurement a little further on, at Lobith Haven. There is also a temporary measuring setup on the other side of the sign that collects data. Squeaks and creaks This is not the first time this year that measurements by Rijkswaterstaat have run into problems on the rivers in the east of the country. A week ago it became known that the rivers there are so low that Rijkswaterstaat's survey boats can no longer get there. Inland shipping skippers now have to decide for themselves whether it is responsible to sail there. Although switching off the sign at Lobith does not cause major problems right away, it is a symbol of a system that is creaking under the extreme drought of recent months. Water experts and climate scientists expect that these kinds of extreme low waters will occur more often in the Netherlands in a changing climate. Rain needed The water discharge at Lobith is currently around 580 cubic metres per second, which remains exceptionally low. When the Rhine will recover is still an open question. That requires a lot of rain, especially further up the Rhine basin in Germany and Switzerland. Rijkswaterstaat had research done into how long it could take before the Rhine again reaches the somewhat more normal discharge of 1000 cubic metres per second, which would still be on the low side. Knowledge institute Deltares established that if conditions are favourable this happens in November or December, but that it cannot be ruled out that it will only be in the new year. It could even be that the Rhine only recovers in the spring.

title: KLM cancels flights, fleet needs maintenance
lead: Airline KLM is cancelling several flights for the coming months. Many aircraft cannot temporarily be used because they are broken. This puts pressure on the fleet. The flights concern the period 26 October to early March. The airline does not yet know how many flights or which destinations are involved. "We are looking at flights with the least impact, where we can rebook as many passengers as possible," says a spokesperson. The airline hopes that by limiting flights early, it can guarantee a more reliable and stable schedule. Renewal The cancellation of the flights is necessary according to KLM due to a combination of circumstances. There is unplanned maintenance and damage repair to aircraft, but also maintenance work that takes longer than expected. For example, delivering parts sometimes takes a long time. In May, the division of KLM that carries out maintenance on aircraft came under enhanced supervision of the <entity id="org:inspectie-leefomgeving-en-transport">Inspectie Leefomgeving en Transport</entity> (ILT). Because the division would not meet new standards that require minor maintenance on aircraft to be handled and recorded more quickly. The airline recently invested seven billion euros in renewing the fleet. At the same time, old models are being phased out. A new type of aircraft, the Airbus A350, recently arrived at Schiphol. "But it takes a while before it is operational," concludes the spokesperson.

title: British navy man suspected of attempted espionage for the Russians
lead: In the United Kingdom, a member of the navy was arrested on Tuesday because he allegedly wanted to pass secret information to the Russians. He was charged today at a court in London. The hearing lasted only four minutes. "As you know, the matters you are charged with are too serious to be dealt with by this court," the judge said. He referred the case to a higher court, the Old Bailey, also in London, where he must appear on 16 October. Wrong from the start The 24-year-old suspect joined the Royal Navy in April 2024; in November of that year he received his first posting on a ship. His task was to gather intelligence for warfare. Because of that role he had access to highly secret information. According to the charge, things went wrong almost immediately. The suspect copied secret information he had access to into his private email account. He also allegedly translated an attempt at contact into Russian and searched the dark web for an address where he could pass information on to Russia. Previously arrested The counter-terrorism police arrested him for the first time last year and again on Tuesday. He has been in custody since then, and that will remain so at least until the hearing next week. The British navy does not wish to comment further on the case. "As long as legal proceedings are ongoing, it would be inappropriate to respond," a spokesperson told the British press.

title: Climate summit in Fiji and Tuvalu largely fails, countries stay away en masse
lead: The preparatory climate summit in Fiji and Tuvalu, co-organised by Australia, has largely ended in failure. From Monday, delegations were invited to these island groups to witness the consequences of the climate crisis. Turnout fell far short. In the end, only two leaders from countries outside the region came to the summit. These were Mauritius and East Timor, which together cause only about 0.02 percent of global emissions. In addition, several ministers and officials from other countries were present. The idea was that world leaders would see these consequences with their own eyes, in order to influence the urgency of reducing emissions and thereby decision-making at the most important climate summit of the year. Slowly under water The delegations that did come saw how in Tuvalu an attempt is being made to create land, because what remains is slowly disappearing under water. Tuvalu is only 26 square kilometres in size and consists of donut-shaped islands where erosion has removed the top of the island and water remains in the middle. On these narrow strips of land, surrounded by an endless sea, only about 11.000 people live. There is no mountain or even a hill in sight, so the rising water swallows more and more land. The expectation is that the country could disappear into the sea by the end of this century. The land reclamation project is a last attempt to survive while the sea level keeps rising. In Fiji, delegations saw how increasing hurricanes and a rising sea level are forcing more and more communities to move. Here - as in many places in the Pacific - a true mass relocation is underway. In Fiji at least 700 communities are in extreme danger due to climate change. The government is moving the most vulnerable villages to higher ground. Island nations in the Pacific are on the front line of the climate crisis. Temperatures here are rising on average faster than in the rest of the world. The sea level is also rising fast. For example, sea level at Suva, the capital of Fiji, has risen by 29 centimetres between 1993 and 2024. This is not only due to climate change; local land subsidence also amplifies the effect. The plan to hold a preparatory climate summit before the big annual UN summit came mainly from Australia. It had lobbied for years to co-host with the Pacific countries this year the major climate conference COP31. But after lengthy diplomatic wrangling, it had to give way to Turkey. The preparatory summit in Fiji and Tuvalu was a compromise. The idea was that world leaders would have the precarious position of the Pacific island states firmly in mind before making agreements at COP31 in Antalya. In Turkey, Australia will also lead the negotiations. Attention of the world But a trip to isolated and hard-to-reach Tuvalu proved too far for many. Still, according to the organisers it is not a complete fiasco. The leaders from the Pacific nevertheless stood side by side with ministers from all over the world, including India, the United Arab Emirates and Turkey. Officials of the United Nations were also present, who have a say on climate finance. "We had said we wanted to draw the world's attention to the problems in the Pacific, particularly those of the small developing island states, and I think we have succeeded in that", said Australian climate minister Chris Bowen. Tuvaluan climate refugees in New Zealand are already noticing that the lack of a future is fading their bond with Tuvalu:

title: Provinces terminate contract with bus operator due to financial problems
lead: The provinces <entity id="org:provincie-flevoland">Flevoland</entity>, <entity id="org:provincie-gelderland">Gelderland</entity> and <entity id="org:provincie-overijssel">Overijssel</entity> are going to prematurely terminate the public transport contract with bus operator EBS. The company was due to provide bus services in large parts of the provinces until the end of 2035, but is facing significant financial losses. The provinces have therefore agreed to end the contract in mid-2029. Due to the shortfalls at the bus operator, the provinces will provide financial support in the coming years to guarantee that the city and regional buses keep running. The provinces do not want to say how much money is involved. The support comes on top of the tens of millions the transport company receives from the provinces each year. Even so, EBS announced earlier this year that it does not have enough money to keep carrying out the 12-year concession, writes Omroep Flevoland. Raised the alarm According to the operator, this is due to "business-related setbacks". For example, EBS is struggling with staff shortages, its electric buses were delivered late, and due to grid shortages there is insufficient capacity to charge buses. EBS has to charge them elsewhere, which leads to extra kilometres for which the company receives no compensation. The operator first raised the alarm with the provinces about this in spring. They then launched an investigation into the company's financial situation. EBS buses have been running in Flevoland and parts of Gelderland and Overijssel since late 2022. The provinces gave the company preference over operators Keolis and Qbuzz. Search for new operator Overijssel and Gelderland are looking for another company that can provide public transport from July 2029. Gelderland wants to set up its own concession for the <entity id="org:gemeente-apeldoorn">Apeldoorn</entity> - Noord-Veluwe area. How bus transport will look from 2029 onwards will be worked out in the coming months. EBS runs multiple public transport concessions across the country and will also provide bus services in <entity id="org:provincie-zeeland">Zeeland</entity>. According to a spokesperson for the company, no losses are being incurred in other parts of the country. "It is purely this concession that is financially out of line, due to a combination of factors. The others are going well." Overloaded grid Also in the <entity id="org:provincie-utrecht">provincie Utrecht</entity>, bus operators Transdev and Keolis are experiencing problems due to the transition to electric buses. Keolis is in talks with the province of Utrecht because the company is making much bigger losses than expected beforehand. Nothing is yet known about the outcome of the talks, writes RTV Utrecht.

title: Latvians arrested at British air force base
lead: British military police arrested two Latvians (36 and 32) overnight who had behaved suspiciously at an RAF air base in the county of Cambridgeshire. They were initially arrested for entering a prohibited area, but later the suspicion was added that they wanted to cause harm to the United Kingdom. Guards at the base near the village of Molesworth discovered an abandoned car around 22.00 hours last night. There was also a small hole in the fence around the base. The two had therefore gone onto the site through it. The Latvians were found and arrested around 02.00 hours. They have been taken to a police station, where the case was handed over to the counter-terrorism unit of the police in London. Fairford In a statement, the head of that unit refers to the arrest last week of five men at the RAF base in Fairford, in the west of England. She understands that this immediately comes to mind, but for now sees no connection with that case. Americans What is striking is that Americans are stationed at the base near Molesworth, according to the BBC. That was also the case at the Fairford base. The American bombers that were stationed there have since left, because they would have been in danger there. According to the BBC, American intelligence services are active at the Molesworth base for operations in Europe and Africa. Searches In connection with the arrest of these Latvians, two addresses in Peterborough have been searched. The British army's explosives disposal service has examined the car that was found, but found nothing unusual.

title: That crazy AI character on TikTok mainly wants you to buy his crypto
lead: A stylishly dressed young Frenchman who calls himself Jean Phil suddenly appears on TikTok and Instagram on 18 September. With his blond bob and curled mustache, he mostly stands around shadowboxing in the videos. Many people find it looks funny. The account attracts tens of millions of views, likes and hundreds of thousands of followers within a few days. He is the trendsetter and a new AI influencer seems to have been born. Jean Phil is trying to monetise this popularity with his own cryptocurrency $ JEANPHIL . Peculiar, realistic-looking AI characters promoting their 'own' cryptocurrency are popping up like mushrooms. They often have the same goal: go viral and get people to buy their homemade cryptocurrency so they can then earn money from it. Recently it has become possible to create such an AI character within a few minutes.
