'Years ago, making this kind of content still required specific skills, such as very good knowledge of video editing', explains crypto expert Bart Mol. 'Now anyone can copy each other directly, and the question of what value such an AI influencer has is becoming more and more relevant.' Via a website, you can relatively easily create your own cryptocurrency: the website takes the technical side of creating such a coin off your hands. The person behind $ JEANPHIL then promotes the cryptocurrency via social media. Genjutsu To create videos on social media that are hard to distinguish from real ones, the website Higgsfield is used, specifically its Genjutsu tool. The website launched its newest toy at the end of August. With the Genjutsu tool you can take an existing video and then adjust it as you wish by replacing characters or specific elements in the video, while the rest remains unchanged. All of that can be done with a few mouse clicks. According to social media expert Kirsten Jassies, more and more of this kind of AI characters are appearing. 'The possibilities with AI are developing so terribly fast. We can barely keep up with it ourselves.' That people can't keep up is evident from the reactions under Jean Phil's videos. Some think it's great, others think it's rubbish. For example, people say they thought for days that Jean Phil was real and hoped so too. Others say they are disappointed in themselves because they only realised late that it was AI, after similar accounts had appeared and the penny dropped. It is not forbidden to launch an AI character on social media, but since August new European legislation has been in force that is meant to better protect people. In many cases a digital watermark must be added to online content if it has been generated by AI. The AI regulation will be rolled out further in the coming years. On the videos on Jean Phil's account, the digital watermark is still barely visible; only one video on both TikTok and Instagram has one. Money from trading After some time, online rumours spread that a pump-and-dump scam would be carried out with the cryptocurrency, but so far that does not appear to be the case. Pump-and-dump means artificially making a cryptocurrency popular, after which the creator sells their coins at a large profit and the price collapses. Since 2024, pump-and-dump schemes with cryptocurrencies have been prohibited. Public data on the $ JEANPHIL coin shows, however, that every time people trade their purchased coins with each other, the creator of the coin keeps a small percentage of that. So far that has reportedly brought the person about 250,000 dollars. 'The creator of the coin will therefore aim to keep trading in the coins alive, because that is how he earns money', Mol adds. At its peak the coin had a total market value of almost eleven million dollars, converted just under ten million euros. After similar accounts appeared online and people realised this was AI, the $ JEANPHIL coin lost a large part of its value.

title: Pro-Hamas expressions at Amsterdam demonstration, would a law have changed anything?
lead: The Amsterdam <entity id="person:femke-halsema">burgemeester Halsema</entity> watched "with great horror" as pro-Palestinian activists chanted slogans such as "Long live the 7th of October", referring to the Hamas attacks in Israel three years ago. They also carried banners with texts such as "We Support Hamas". The demonstration was not banned, however, until activists ran into a police cordon elsewhere in the city. Why only then? Four questions about this demonstration: Could the demonstration have been banned because of the slogans? What the demonstrators showed was "shocking and distasteful", said Mayor Halsema on behalf of the <entity id="org:openbaar-ministerie">Openbaar Ministerie</entity> and the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> in a response, but it was not punishable. And so she could not intervene. A spokesperson for the Amsterdam OM explains: "According to the OM's position there was no incitement; the expressions do not encourage people to commit criminal offences." A bill is in the works that makes glorifying terrorism punishable, he adds. "It could well be that some expressions made last night will be punishable once this bill becomes law. But to really say something about that we have to await the text of the law. It will always have to be determined per situation and depending on the context whether something is punishable or not." "A mayor is not concerned with the content of a demonstration", professor of constitutional and administrative law Jon Schilder tells the NOS. "She may only look at whether disorder threatens. And only then may she intervene." Halsema therefore acted correctly by not banning the demonstration outright at the start, he believes. Why was the demonstration nevertheless banned at some point? That is due to fear of disorder. The activists walked from the Dam in a different direction than they had initially announced, towards a place where many buildings of Jewish significance stand, such as the Jewish Museum, the Holocaust Names Monument and the Portuguese Synagogue. Officers stopped the some 75 activists at the Waterlooplein and said they were only allowed to walk to the town hall, the local broadcaster AT5 writes. Some of the demonstrators tried to break through the line of police officers, which did not succeed. The entire demonstration was then dissolved by Mayor Halsema. This briefly led to unrest between demonstrators and police. What would a new law have changed? Last summer a bill went to <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity> that makes glorifying terrorist offences punishable, both personally and by distributing videos or images with that intent. Expressions of support for banned terrorist organisations will also be prohibited once the law takes effect. A banner reading 'We Support Hamas', as seen on the Dam yesterday, would no longer be allowed after the proposed law is introduced, says Schilder. "Such banners will, like Hamas flags, fall within the scope of this bill. That is something that will actually change if this law is introduced." Even if that law were already in force, it still would not have meant that Mayor Halsema could have banned the demonstration on 7 October in advance, says professor Schilder. "Preventive action is not possible." Only when, for example, a Hamas flag is unfurled can the police intervene and arrest people. What would the punishment have been then? The penalties attached to it are not trivial, he believes: a maximum of two years' imprisonment and a fine. Because it is a criminal offence, a violation would also result in a criminal record. But, he warns, "it is an open question whether the OM gets to it at all: due to understaffing they have to leave many cases unattended. Whether they will prosecute cases like these is therefore partly a political choice too." Another potential problem with the law is that, in his view, "the line is not clear" where glorification of terrorism begins. For example, the banner reading 'Long live the seventh of October' shown in Amsterdam yesterday would be a difficult case for the criminal court. "That is a grey area, because it is not clear what exactly is meant by that date." "It is not black and white. In that respect it is a bit reminiscent of the 'fewer Moroccans' statement by <entity id="person:geert-wilders">Geert Wilders</entity>. That was debated for years, until the <entity id="org:hoge-raad">Hoge Raad</entity> said: that was punishable." In the same way, he warns, you cannot say in advance whether something is or is not punishable when it comes to glorifying terrorism. "The criminal judge will not quickly reach a conviction."

title: Christa Pike can walk again but is 'angry and confused', lawyers say
lead: The death row inmate Christa Pike can walk a little again. One of her lawyers said this to the British broadcaster BBC. The American woman is still in hospital in a hazy state. Pike's lawyer Stephen Ferrell tells the BBC that he has not spoken to her directly, but understood that her arms were swollen and that she could barely function when she took her first steps in the hospital room. The 50-year-old Pike was due to be executed by lethal injection in the American state of Tennessee last week, but it failed twice. She was convicted in 1996 of the murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. According to the non-profit organization Death Penalty Information Center, Pike is the first person to survive her death sentence by lethal injection. 'Angry and confused' Yesterday another lawyer of Pike said that she was "angry and confused" when she regained consciousness, but that she is very aware "that the state has tried to execute her". The first thing she asked after waking up was "where am I and who are you?", says her other lawyer Randy Spivey. According to Spivey there was a lot of confusion with Pike and she wants to know what has happened. "She asked about her team, she asked about the family of the victim." The lawyer also said that Pike could not move her arms and could not swallow either. She also has pneumonia and a blood clot in one of her arms. Evidence What exactly went wrong during the execution is still unclear and is being investigated. A judge in Nashville yesterday ordered the state to preserve "everything that was in the room itself" as evidence of the failed execution attempt. According to her lawyers, Pike is handcuffed to the bed by one hand and her feet. The lawyers have asked the judge whether, given the injuries, she may be unshackled. The hospital staff reportedly requested this. The judge only wants to decide on that once the affidavit is submitted, American media write. Her lawyers also argued that Pike has suffered enough and want the governor of Tennessee to commute her death sentence to life without the possibility of parole. Execution carried out in Texas Yesterday the first execution in the US since Pike's was carried out. In the state of Texas the 46-year-old Jamaal Howard was put to death by lethal injection. Howard had been convicted of the murder of a shop employee during a robbery in 2000. He was 20 years old at the time. Shortly before the lethal injection with pentobarbital was administered, Howard apologised to the family members of the victim who were present at the execution. "I'm sorry for what happened. I hope you can forgive me one day." He also thanked his family and friends. The man took a few breaths and gasped for air when the drug began to work. Then he made snoring sounds and coughed, with the sound growing softer each time. Howard was pronounced dead nineteen minutes after the injection, at 20.03 hours.

title: Fake agent gets four years in prison after rape of international student
lead: The court in The Hague has sentenced a man to four years in prison for raping an international student. The 33-year-old man from The Hague, Ghalied A., posed as a police officer to gain access to the victim. A. rang the student's doorbell on the night of 12 September 2024; she was then living in a student complex in The Hague. He was reportedly tipped off that there were drugs in her room and, by his own account, came to check. The South Korean student, who had been in the Netherlands for only a month, did not know the rules and procedures and let the man in. Once inside, the woman had to stand naked with her hands against the wall and bend her knees a few times, after which the man sexually assaulted her. Immediately after the incident the victim locked herself in the bathroom and called 112. The officers who arrived at the scene found her naked and crying. Returned to South Korea According to the court, the woman had dreamed her whole life of studying in Europe. After the incident she reportedly developed such a dislike of the Netherlands that she returned directly to South Korea. The court found the victim's statements concrete, detailed and consistent. The suspect's statement was set aside. The man from The Hague maintained that the two of them had started talking outside <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de kamer</entity> and that she had invited him in. Public indecency A few months after the incident, the man tried again to strike in exactly the same way. Again he rang the doorbells of the same student complexes and posed as a police officer. This time nobody opened the door. The suspect is also guilty of public indecency in another student complex. Last year he allegedly exposed his genitals in public there and openly masturbated. The OM had demanded five years in prison and a TBS order with compulsory admission. The judge decided not to impose TBS because the man refused to cooperate with psychological research. However, extra supervision of the man will be maintained after his prison sentence.

title: Heavy smoke from fire in parking garage under Olympic Stadium
lead: A fire broke out in the parking garage under the Olympic Stadium in Amsterdam last night. A lot of smoke was released in the fire. The fire broke out around 18.30 hours in the crawl space of the parking garage. The fire brigade has not said whether any cars were on fire. Among other things, foam was used to fight the fire. Because the seat of the fire was difficult to reach, extinguishing it took a long time. Around 00.38 hours the fire was under control. The area around the stadium was cordoned off, the regional broadcaster NH writes. The safety region called on residents to close windows and doors if they were bothered by the smoke.

title: Maduro and wife charged with torturing opponents and Americans
lead: Captured Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores have both been served with a new indictment in the United States. They are now also accused of having tortured political opponents and American citizens to maintain their grip on power in the South American country. They were previously prosecuted for, among other things, corruption and facilitating large-scale international cocaine trafficking. Flores (69) and Maduro (63) were abducted from Venezuela by the American army on 3 January and taken to New York. They pleaded not guilty to the drug charges and have been held since their arrest at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn. Their trial is scheduled for 1 June 2027. Electric shocks News agency Reuters reports that Maduro and Flores risk a mandatory minimum sentence of 50 years in prison if they are found guilty. The US and human rights groups have for some time accused Venezuelan officials of the Maduro regime of torturing prisoners. Today's indictment is the first time Maduro is being criminally prosecuted for those allegations. According to the indictment, an American citizen was arrested in Venezuela in 2022 and accused of conspiring to murder Maduro. The man was reportedly tortured by military counterintelligence officers with blows and electric shocks to his arms, legs and genitals. Heart operation In another case, prosecutors state that in 2013 Maduro ordered the arrest of a Venezuelan soldier whom he suspected of planning a coup. During interrogations, the officer was reportedly repeatedly beaten, among other things with a power cable. Today the judge rejected a request to release Flores from prison due to health problems. Flores' lawyers argued that she needs heart surgery and proposed moving her to a home with 24-hour security. They said she poses no danger to society. The prosecutors argued that Flores receives adequate medical care at the detention center in New York and that she is an extreme flight risk. When rejecting the request, the judge said the evidence against Flores was substantial. Prosecutors say she accepted hundreds of thousands of dollars in bribes from a major drug baron.

title: Searches of homes of ex-prince Andrew unlawful, but investigation continues
lead: A small win for the British ex-prince Andrew. A court in London agrees with him that the police made important mistakes in February when searching his homes in Sandringham and Windsor. The search warrants were based on the wrong statutory article. The court therefore declared the warrants unlawful. This does not mean the investigation against him must now be stopped, the court said. The searches were related to the investigation into whether the ex-prince, while he was British trade envoy (2001-2011), shared secret information with the American sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Errors acknowledged: Andrew (66), who now goes by the name Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor as a private citizen, went to the judge to have the search warrants declared unlawful. He presumably hoped that any evidence found during the searches could not be used against him. Whether that reasoning holds up is still the question. The police do not yet have to return the prince's seized property. The court will consider next year whether material taken during the searches may still be used as evidence. Andrew did not appear in court himself, possibly partly because he knew how this would turn out. The police had already admitted in July that errors were made in drafting the search warrants, but had not yet made this public.

title: Gold Televizier-Ring for De Bondgenoten, presenter Jan Versteegh also wins
lead: The Gold Televizier-Ring 2026 was won by the SBS6 reality game series De Bondgenoten. The choice of the Dutch viewer was announced by veteran TV presenter Henny Huisman. The other nominees were consumer programme Kassa of BNNVARA and the Twente drama series Woeste Grond of AVROTROS. Presenter Jan Versteegh of De Bondgenoten also won the Televizier-Ring for best presenter. Other nominees were Thomas van Groningen and Tim Hofman. Annet Malherbe won the Televizier-ring for best actor. She received it for her role as Emma in Rust en Vreugd. That drama series was about a newly widowed woman who gets a small garden in an allotment complex. There she becomes involved in the mutual feuds and vendettas. PaardenpraatTV The prize for Televizier-Ring Talent, the audience prize for up-and-coming TV talent, went to interior stylist and TV personality Daan Alferink. He beat radio maker Bram Krikke and WNL presenter Frank van Leeuwen. Just before that, PaardenpraatTV won the Gold Televizier-Ring Youth for the most popular children's programme. The YouTube channel about horses is presented, among others, by Britt Dekker. Britt Dekker was in ecstasy when she received the award: The BNNVARA programme Even Tot Hier won the Televizier Ring Impact, the prize for the TV programme, TV moment or documentary with the most social impact. The programme raised more than 3 million euros for war-stricken Ukraine. It did so by repeatedly drawing attention to the foundation of Ukrainian accordionist Oleg. With the money raised, ambulances and medical equipment could be bought. Andy in de Auto won the Televizier-Ring Online video series. In that programme former footballer Andy van der Meijde has conversations with a variety of guests in his car. Van der Meijde's series beat Opdracht of StukTV and Tobi's Eetclub, by Tobias Camman, who previously won the prize for the FOMO Show.

title: Four astronauts back on Earth after 237 days, record for European woman
lead: Four astronauts have returned to Earth after eight months from the International Space Station ISS. SpaceX brought the crew back safely in a space capsule. The so-called splashdown took place off the coast of Los Angeles. After the capsule was hoisted aboard a recovery ship, the four came out. "Finally showering again," one of the astronauts said on return. The crew consisted of two Americans, a Russian and a Frenchwoman. They were brought to the space station in February on an urgent basis to replace four other crew members. Those had been sent home early after one of them fell ill. It was NASA's first medical evacuation in 65 years. The astronauts were actually supposed to return earlier. That did not go ahead because the new batch of astronauts arrived at the ISS three weeks later than planned. Their space capsule had a leak in the fuel supply and first had to be repaired. The space trip lasted 237 days in total. With this, French astronaut Sophie Adenot set a record: never before has a European astronaut stayed in space so long without interruption. Maintenance on the space station During her stay, Adenot carried out three spacewalks to perform maintenance on the space station, which is now almost 28 years old. With this she is the second European woman to leave the space station during her stay. The new crew, who arrived last week, also set an American record. They reached the ISS in eight hours, much shorter than the old American record of 12.5 hours. They will stay in space for about half a year. At this moment there are seven astronauts in the space station, from the United States, Canada and Russia.

title: Well-preserved fossil reveals how mammals ate differently from dinosaurs
lead: A well-preserved fossil 165 million years old shows scientists how mammals developed a new way of swallowing during the time of the dinosaurs. The find is so well preserved that the outline of the animal is clearly visible and even imprints of its skin and fur are recognisable. The fossil was found in China a few years ago. It concerns an animal that resembled a cross between a beaver and a platypus, with the flat, scaly tail of a beaver and the powerful swimming feet of the platypus. With its weight of 1 to 2 kilos and length of 50 centimetres, it was a sizeable youngster at a time when most mammals were not much bigger than a mouse. Referring to its large tail, scientists named the animal Megacauda sungei . Although the animal resembles two current species, there are no descendants of it left today. Because the fossil is so well preserved after the carcass ended up in river mud, the animal's hyoid bone also remained preserved. That is often not found because it is small and fragile and, unlike other bones, does not connect to other bones. This find sheds more light on how these early mammals had a different way of eating from the dominant reptiles of the time. Because their bone was more complex than in dinosaurs, mammals can use their mouth muscles to chew food and swallow it in small amounts. Reptiles, by contrast, gulp down their prey in large bites, as crocodiles do, or swallow it in one piece, like a snake. The scientists explain how this development gave mammals an advantage. "Thanks to this feature, different species could develop specific teeth and tap into a variety of food sources. They could become carnivores, insectivores, herbivores, omnivores and everything in between." Evolutionary innovation This led, after the dinosaurs went extinct 66 million years ago, to mammals being able to develop into the new dominant animal species. "It was an enormous evolutionary innovation. Mammals all swallow equally efficiently and effortlessly." The hyoid bone was also crucial for swallowing when suckling young. In the case of Megacauda, the researchers found that its diet consisted of salamanders. Evidence for this was partially digested vertebrae they found in its stomach and skeletons of these prey animals in the same soil layer. They infer from this that this Megacauda must have lived partly in the water, where it hunted like an otter. To avoid meeting meat-eating dinosaurs, it was probably a nocturnal animal, which spent the day in burrows on the riverbank.

title: Thousands of supporters arrested, according to Indian Cockroach movement
lead: Indian authorities have arrested thousands of supporters of the Cockroach movement, the movement says on social media. It is unclear how many people have been arrested in total. No independent source confirms the figures. Prominent members such as spokesperson Deepak Baliyan are also reported to have been arrested the day before a large protest in the capital New Delhi. For days, demonstrations have been held in India over a controversial revision of the electoral rolls. As a result, according to the activists, millions of Indians risk being unable to vote in future elections. The activists demand the departure of the head of the Indian election commission, Gyanesh Kumar. The election commission says the revision is needed to remove, among other things, invalid registrations, but according to opponents, mainly minorities, particularly Muslims, are losing their right to vote. In the state of West Bengal, millions of people have already lost their voting rights. Opponents also see the revision as an attempt to secure future election victories for the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) of Prime Minister Modi. Opposition parties and prominent politicians such as Rahul Gandhi have also joined the protests. What is the Cockroach movement? The Cockroach movement is a prominent movement in the ongoing wave of public discontent with the government of Indian Prime Minister Modi. The actions began with calls for education reform after a major exam fraud scandal. Indirectly, that scandal cost the lives of more than twenty students who committed suicide due to psychological pressure. For days, thousands of students therefore took to the streets to demand the departure of the Minister of Education. That minister has since resigned. The protest movement embraced the name 'Cockroaches' after a judge had labelled its supporters that way. The judge called young people without education or jobs who engage in activism or journalism cockroaches and parasites. According to the Cockroach movement, a group of students from the western city of Pune was arrested and taken by bus to an unknown location. The group was on its way to the protest against the revision in New Delhi on Saturday. Daliyan was also reportedly taken to an unknown location. According to the movement, he and his brother were severely beaten by the Indian police. The movement demands their release.

title: Off, then not, now on again: rainbow flag will after all hang at the House of Representatives
lead: A majority of the House of Representatives is in favour of flying a rainbow flag in front of the House of Representatives building on Sunday, on Coming Out Day. That emerged on Thursday evening during a roll-call vote. During the late Thursday evening vote in the House of Representatives, 90 members were in favour of raising it and 36 were against. It is the first time this flag will be seen in front of the House of Representatives. The members voted individually, but it was clear that most members from D66, VVD, CDA, Pro, Partij voor de Dieren, SP, ChristenUnie, 50Plus and Volt voted in favour. The members from JA21 and the group-Markuszower were not present. PVV, Forum voor Democratie, Denk and SGP were against. Heated discussion. Whether or not to raise the rainbow flag has led to quite a heated discussion behind the scenes in the House of Representatives in recent days. Initially the presidium, the daily board of the House of Representatives, thought it was a good idea, but on second thoughts it scrapped the plan after all, RTL Nieuws reported earlier today. This happened after small Christian parties had been informed of the new flag plan. It met with resistance from the Christian opposition party SGP. Only larger parties sit on the presidium, but the intention is that the views of smaller parties are taken into account. On 24 February 2024 the Ukrainian flag was hoisted in front of the House of Representatives building, two years after the Russian invasion. The SGP believes that flags other than the Dutch flag should be hoisted with restraint. "The rainbow flag is not a national flag, but a flag of interest groups that has since grown into a symbol of activism", said SGP member of parliament Van Dijk. A number of opposition parties such as Pro, Partij voor de Dieren, 50Plus and Volt were so outraged that they submitted a motion to try to reverse the decision. "The House of Representatives must stand up for the rights of the worldwide LGBTI movement", the members stated in the motion. They also wrote in the motion that it is important that there is "an inclusive working environment" for the staff of the House of Representatives. The motion had to be put to a roll-call vote late on Thursday evening as well, at the insistence of the SGP. This meant that each member individually, not by parliamentary group, made their position known. U-turn. All members had to be called back for that roll-call vote. So various members who had already gone home on Thursday had to turn back. And that caused considerable irritation. A waste of thousands of kilometres, said BBB member Van der Plas, who had come back from her home town of Deventer. CU member Grinwis called the whole affair "sad and ridiculous", but did vote for the motion. "For the sake of the people it concerns."

title: Pentagon wants to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan by firing squad
lead: The US Department of Defense wants to livestream the execution of a man who killed thirteen people in 2009. It would be the first public execution in the US in ninety years. Nidal Hasan was a major and worked in the American army as a psychiatrist. Because he was a soldier and shot people at a military base, he is being executed by the army. Last Tuesday it was already revealed that this would be carried out by firing squad. Now the Pentagon also reports that it can be watched live by Americans. 3 December The execution is scheduled for 3 December, but due to appeal procedures it is questionable whether that date will be met. "We are going to do it on a Thursday, at 13.00 hours, when he committed his act", says Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth: If the execution is indeed to be viewable via livestream, it is probably the first time since 1936 that a large public can watch an execution. Almost always an execution in the US is only viewable by a limited group of people such as lawyers, family members of victims and a small group of media representatives. Approved by Trump The firing squad execution of Hasan has been approved by President Trump, which is required for military executions. The Pentagon gives no further details about broadcasting the execution and, when asked by CNN among others, only states that "the execution will be livestreamed". It is the first time since 1961 that the American army carries out the death penalty. It is also very rare for a convicted person in the US to be executed by firing squad. That has happened only six times since 1977, out of 1684 executions. By far most death row inmates received a lethal injection. Hasan opened fire in a building on the Texas army base Fort Hood where American soldiers were medically examined. In doing so, the American of Palestinian descent shouted "allahu akbar". The soldiers who were examined there were to be deployed to Afghanistan. Besides the thirteen dead, more than thirty people were injured in the attack.

title: French minister announces emergency plan after protests: 3000 substitute teachers
lead: The French Minister of Education has announced an emergency plan in response to the ongoing protests in France. In the short term, he wants to deploy more than 3000 extra teachers. According to Minister Geffray, the teachers must start work at the 514 schools where the teacher shortage is greatest. According to the minister, most of them can start by next Tuesday. In addition, Geffray and French Prime Minister Lecornu announced that money is being set aside to temporarily hire staff after the autumn holiday, which in France runs from 17 October to 2 November. 'Not very convincing' Whether the measures will calm the protests is an open question. "Édouard Geffray tries to offer reassurance....without really convincing anyone", is the headline in Le Parisien, for example. And Le Monde says it is mainly a stopgap, with the question being whether shortages will still arise later in the year. The teachers' union SNES-FSU calls it "a hasty attempt to create the appearance of a political solution, but one that is not sustainable". For further measures, the government points to the 2027 budget. Lecornu wants to make a change to it in which he can free up extra budget to further absorb shortages. 71,500 demonstrators Yesterday there were again demonstrations in many places by secondary school pupils. University students also joined. According to the ministry of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-biza">Binnenlandse Zaken</entity>, 71,500 people took to the streets yesterday. Those marches and blockades were largely peaceful, but in some places there were also violent outbursts alongside the peaceful demonstrations. In Strasbourg, for example, a police car was set on fire, and in Bordeaux arson was committed at a police station. During the protests, 504 arrests were made yesterday and 48 police officers were injured. Calm in Liège The protests have also spread to Belgium. There, in recent days, protests have been held against planned cuts to education. In Liège, the protests caused damage, after which a ban on assembly took effect yesterday. As a result of this and of stricter controls, according to the Liège police it was a quiet day yesterday. No damage was done and the city centre was calm. However, 76 people were arrested, probably because they did not comply with the ban on assembly.

title: Terneuzen municipal council agrees to permit for asylum seekers' centre
lead: After a debate lasting hours, the Terneuzen municipal council last night agreed late in the evening to a permit for an asylum seekers' centre. The previous council was still against it. That was reason for then mayor <entity id="person:erik-van-merrienboer">Erik van Merrienboer</entity> to step down. The new college of mayor and aldermen, which was installed in July, adjusted the proposal to improve social safety. The focus was placed more on reception for families. The new proposal was narrowly adopted with the support of some opposition parties: there were sixteen votes in favour and fourteen against. Former office building That means the <entity id="org:zbo-centraal-orgaan-opvang-asielzoekers">COA</entity> can get to work on realising an asylum centre on Handelspoort in a former office building. Terneuzen will accommodate a maximum of 200 people. After the vote, the PVV submitted a motion of no confidence against all aldermen. This caused displeasure with mayor Weerwind, who sternly addressed the council according to Omroep <entity id="org:provincie-zeeland">Zeeland</entity>: "Difficult files are coming, and even then we must take our responsibility." The motion was rejected with 18 votes against and 12 in favour.

title: Morning briefing 9/10: Announcement of the Nobel Peace Prize • Last day to hand in fireworks anonymously
lead: Good morning! Today is the last day you can hand in fireworks anonymously, and in Oslo the winner of the Nobel Peace Prize will be announced. First, the weather: it will be changeable, with the most rain in the west and north of the country. A strong southwesterly wind is blowing, with gusts up to 75 km/h in coastal regions. It will be 14 to 18 degrees. Saturday and Sunday it stays changeable, but the sun also shines. With slightly less wind, it will be around 15 degrees in the afternoon. Are you heading out today? Here you can find the overview of traffic jams and roadworks, and here everything about the situation on the rail network. What can you expect today? What did you miss? The American Department of Defense wants to livestream the execution of a man who killed thirteen people in 2009. This would therefore probably be the first public execution in the US in ninety years. The execution is scheduled for 3 December and will be carried out by a firing squad. Other news from overnight: And then one more thing: In the building of the European Parliament in Strasbourg, a remarkable statue has been unveiled. The 2.6-meter-high artwork shows a naked Donald Trump and is called The Orange Plague. The statue by Danish artist Jens Galschiøt is covered in gold leaf and is intended as a satirical protest against the American president. Galschiøt, who regards Trump as a great danger to the international legal order, was inspired by the fairy tale The Emperor's New Clothes. In the well-known story, a vain leader thinks he is walking around in the finest clothes, but in reality he is naked. The statue is part of a three-day exhibition organised by the Danish party in the European Parliament, the Left group. Have a nice day!

title: Rising French national debt and interest rate increasingly worrying for Europe
lead: Under pressure from ongoing demonstrations, the French government has promised that 3000 extra teachers will be hired. But the pressure on France to address its public finances is at least as great. France has, since the French Revolution of 1789, a tradition of mass protests that escalate into violence. And, to mention two recent examples, whether it concerns investing in school buildings or reversing pension cuts: meeting the demands of the demonstrators costs the state money. Money that does not exist. "The task of cutting spending was already very large, but because of rising interest rates it is becoming much harder still", says Rabobank economist Maartje Wijffelaars. According to a panel of economists appointed by the French government, 126 billion euros must be cut to stabilize the national debt by 2032. "That will hurt", says Wijffelaars, "because you cannot spare all households and businesses". France's debt mountain. France structurally spends more than it takes in, and also more than the EU's stability pact allows. And so French national debt keeps rising. According to the latest European statistics it amounts to just over 3500 billion euros. France's debt has risen to 119 percent of GDP (the total annual national income). A debt of at most 60 percent is considered desirable in the EU. France has repeatedly been reprimanded by the EU over its high budget deficit and high national debt. Declining confidence. Investors are also looking critically at France. Confidence that the country can repay its debts in the long term is falling. This is shown by the rising interest rate on government debt. Anyone lending money to France for 10 years now gets almost 5 percent interest per year. One and a half years ago that was still 3.5 percent. Investors demand a higher interest rate because they doubt France's creditworthiness. And so the country is not only dealing with high debt, but interest is also taking an ever larger bite out of the budget. France correspondent Saskia Houttuin: "While French debts and interest costs keep rising, <entity id="org:regering">de regering</entity> of Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu is in a tight spot. In the coming period he must get the 2027 budget through parliament. But just as in the Netherlands, the government has no majority. Last year that already proved a huge challenge, but Lecornu got through it thanks to a deal with the socialists. This year it will be harder; with the presidential elections on the horizon, opposition parties will not readily want to get burned by unpopular cuts. Lecornu does have one trump card; he could possibly push the budget through without parliament. But earlier, the use of that controversial legal provision led to a government collapse, so it is also a risk." Also other countries have a very high national debt, such as the United Kingdom and the United States. Even the Netherlands and Germany are seeing interest rates rise. But in France the rate is rising a lot faster. That interest rate difference, called the 'spread', was still 0.8 percent a year ago. It is now 1.5 percent. "That may seem little, but it is a cause for concern", says ING economist Bert Colijn. Given the size of the national debt, it concerns billions. "If that difference becomes too large, it leads to doubts among investors, banks and other countries about the strength of the entire European Union", Colijn explains. Eurocrisis. That recalls 2010, when the Greek debt crisis erupted. Greece's huge debt led to declining confidence in the euro. After lengthy crisis talks the EU provided emergency loans to the country. That ensured Europe stayed politically together and the euro did not sink further. In recent weeks too the euro has lost value against the dollar. The question is whether the situation now is as serious as it was in 2010. Colijn says the situation is still far from as pressing as it was then with Greece, but the consequences if France slides further are potentially greater. "France is a much bigger player than Greece, both politically and economically. If France weakens financially further, it will affect the whole of Europe more than Greece did back then." According to Colijn, the pressure on the European Central Bank to step in may increase, but it is really first up to France itself to solve its problems.

title: Two inspectors in Germany shot dead during weapons check, 60-year-old man arrested
lead: A routine weapons check in the German state of Bavaria completely got out of hand. Two local inspectors, according to German media a 54-year-old woman and a 45-year-old man, were shot dead by the 60-year-old resident of the house where the check took place. The police have arrested the suspect. This lasted for hours. After the man had killed the officials, he barricaded himself in his home in the village of Berngau. To keep the police out, he had blocked his house. The police moved out with many units yesterday afternoon at around 14.00 hours and surrounded the house with specialist teams and an armoured vehicle. A police helicopter also flew over the home. Neighbours were asked to stay indoors. Meanwhile the police kept telephone contact with the man. When he continued to refuse to come out, the arrest units forced their way into the home around 03.00 hours last night. Explosives were used and shots were fired directly at the suspect. The 60-year-old was slightly wounded in the leg by a bullet during his arrest. 'Died immediately' It is unclear why the man shot the officials. The local police report that the check was a standard procedure in which it would be checked, for example, whether the man's weapons permits were in order and whether his weapons were stored correctly. There was no intention to confiscate the weapons. Initially the police reported that the male inspector had died and the woman had been seriously injured. This was later corrected. A police spokesperson says: "We assume she died immediately as a result of the shooting." About the shooter's motive, he does not wish to say anything further, Der Spiegel writes.

title: ICE shoots man in car in New York, with 5-year-old child in back seat
lead: The American immigration service ICE has shot a man in his car in the city of New York. According to mayor Mamdani, a 5-year-old child was also in the car. The man was taken to hospital with unknown injuries; the child was unharmed. The shooting quickly led to protests from local residents and politicians. Mamdani says ICE agents first surrounded the car and then fired shots. The Department of Homeland Security is providing little information about the incident, except that it concerns a man from the Dominican Republic without valid documents. He is also said to have ties to a gang. Condemnation Mamdani condemns the shooting in strong terms. In a statement he calls it "an unacceptable and very serious situation". He also says he will call President Trump. "I will then demand that all ICE actions in our city be stopped. I will no longer stand by while ICE agents terrorise our communities." "ICE must disappear from our neighbourhoods," the statement by Mamdani continues. "ICE must disappear from our hospitals. ICE must disappear from our streets. ICE must stay away from our children." The mayor concludes with: "Abolish ICE." Other local politicians also expressed their outrage. For example, the district chair of The Bronx, where the incident took place, said: "ICE, get out!" She also encouraged the crowd to resist the immigration service. Demonstrations Shortly after the shooting, demonstrators gathered around the scene of the incident. They carried signs with texts such as: "All murdering ICE agents must go to prison" and "Leave our neighbours alone". A large group of people also gathered at the hospital where the victim is being treated. There, a confrontation broke out between demonstrators and the police. Since President Trump began his second term in the White House, the immigration services ICE and CBP (Customs and Border Protection) have arrested tens of thousands of people. Dozens of people have also been shot, with at least eleven deaths. Dozens of people arrested by ICE have died in detention centres, where people are held in appalling conditions.

title: Rotterdam woman (23) was driving herself during fatal accident in Aruba, says Public Prosecution Service
lead: The Rotterdam woman (23) who died last month in a single-vehicle accident in Aruba was herself behind the wheel of the off-road vehicle. That is the conclusion of the <entity id="org:openbaar-ministerie">Openbaar Ministerie</entity> in Aruba, based on video footage. The woman's family members told Rijnmond earlier that they could not imagine the woman was driving herself. Kimberly van Ardenne was on holiday on the island with her boyfriend. Together with a Dutch marine who lives on the island, they set off on Sunday afternoon, 13 September, in a UTV, an open off-road vehicle. For reasons still unknown, the off-road vehicle overturned. The two male occupants remained unharmed. The woman died on the spot. The men told local authorities that Kimberly was behind the wheel, but family members in the Netherlands doubted that. "She falls more into the category of scaredy-cats than daredevils," her cousin Stephanie told Rijnmond. The woman reportedly already experienced a lot of stress in the Netherlands when driving in the morning rush hour or parking in traffic jams. 'Public attention' Justice in Aruba now says that the account of the two other occupants is correct. The investigation has not yet been concluded. But because of the "public attention", justice is already making this information public now. The family's lawyer, Peter Schouten, says in a statement on X that he finds it "extremely strange" that justice is now releasing the information about the video. "The family also finds it cruel and inhuman that this video was not shown to them immediately, and that their grief was therefore unnecessarily disturbed for four weeks by the uncertainty about Kimberly's death," he writes.

title: Americans protest against sexual violence: 'Done with protecting the elite'
lead: In dozens of American cities, people have taken to the streets against sexual violence. What began as anger over the rape case at the prestigious Cornell University has grown into something bigger. Demonstrators want accountability and justice, "from the student house to the White House". In Washington, D.C., hundreds of people gathered last night. "How many young women do we silence to protect the future of 'promising young men'?" activist Cheyenne Hunt asks the crowd. "Zero!" is the answer. Jane Doe The demonstrators across the country expressed their support for Jane Doe. This is the name given to the anonymous student who has filed a case because, by her own account, she was raped two years ago by students of Cornell. The alleged perpetrators, seven members of a student fraternity, were not punished or were only lightly punished by the university. "I am furious", says Grace Wankelman, one of the organizers of the protest in D.C. "And not only about what happened at Cornell. There are countless stories of perpetrators who get away with sexual violence without justice being done for the victim." "I am also Jane Doe", she adds. At the age of seventeen she was raped by a man she trusted. "When I started crying after I couldn't get him off me, he said that at least I could pretend I enjoyed it too." A signal to boys "He said those words six months after Trump, who boasts about 'grabbing women by the pussy', was elected president. What signal does that send to boys when a rapist holds the most powerful position in the country?" "It shows that they can use women as objects without consequences, because they are promising young men", Wankelman believes. "But what about the promising young women?" Demonstrators speak of a system in which the elite, from 'the Cornell Seven' to Jeffrey Epstein, is protected at the expense of victims. "It is part of a larger pattern of institutions protecting their reputation instead of people", says Epstein victim Dani Benski at the protest. "Powerful men are protected, while victims have to fight to prove what happened to them and to be believed." With the nationwide protests, they are asking not only for justice for 'Jane Doe' and the victims of Epstein, but also for better protection for victims of sexual violence. Trump recently changed the rules for handling complaints about sexual misconduct at schools and universities, to the dismay of advocates for victims. 'Men look away' "Many men choose to look away", thinks Kim from Virginia. "To listen to inappropriate jokes and comments and not speak out against them. That is why it is important that we are all here." A male student at the protest agrees with her. "If we as men do not speak out and support women, we leave intact the system that makes this terrible behavior possible. That is why we all need to take to the streets." From the Washington Monument, the demonstrators move toward the White House. Shelly Kohl from Tennessee is angry, but also glad to be there. "I realize I am not alone. There are many victims, and hearing their stories makes me feel less alone." In front of the White House, the group shouts for justice for Jane Doe and for all victims of sexual violence. "Nine years ago I lost the fight with my rapist, but I will not lose this fight", Wankelman promises. "I will not stop fighting until the perpetrators are driven out of positions of power." Podcast De Dag: Jane Doe and the uprising against elite university Cornell Listen here: You can listen to this episode of De Dag via NPO Luister and all other podcast apps. Do you like it? Then don't forget to subscribe.

title: Former prime minister Schoof: 'US Ukraine policy no longer possible to follow after Trump took office'
lead: From the moment Donald Trump entered the White House for the second time, American policy regarding Ukraine could no longer be followed. That is what former prime minister Dick Schoof says in the podcast De Atlantische Blik. The plans of the European allies repeatedly made little progress because the US withdrew time and again at the last moment. After President Trump made clear that the US would not support Ukraine unconditionally, a large number of European countries set up the coalition of the willing. In order to take a leading role regarding Ukraine's security. Schoof, who took part in the talks on behalf of the Netherlands, says that the leaders of the European countries took important steps several times to protect Ukraine at the moment there would be a ceasefire or deal. "But every time that slipped through our fingers," says Schoof. "Because the American negotiators, who had a direct line to the White House, sometimes made a backward movement again while they had previously made a forward one." Schoof specifically mentions Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. This pair is constantly deployed by Trump on the international stage. Kushner is Trump's son-in-law, Witkoff is a friend of the president from the real estate world. According to Schoof, the change of guard in Washington has had a great impact. "Especially on international relations. Trump and Putin also performed a kind of dance that was very difficult for Europe to follow. It then turned out that European security is simply not the first priority for the US. That lies much more in China." Zelensky also unhappy with US The statements by Schoof come at the moment that Ukrainian President Zelensky also says that the US no longer offers help in the fight against Russia. According to Zelensky, the Americans cannot improve economic ties with Russia and mediate in the war at the same time. Recently Russia has been increasing the number of attacks on Ukraine. Civilians are increasingly losing their lives as a result. According to President Zelensky, more than 130 people lost their lives in Russian attacks in the past few days alone. Zelensky has asked the US to give Ukraine more access to Starlink satellites. This would allow the country to defend itself better against Russian ballistic missiles. According to Zelensky, Putin will come to the negotiating table when Ukraine has the upper hand in the air.

title: Peace prize for South African human rights chief and ICC judge Navi Pillay
lead: The Nobel Peace Prize this year goes to South African judge Navi Pillay. From 2003 to 2008 she was a judge at the International Criminal Court (ICC), and from 2008 to 2014 she was United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights. She is currently active for the International Court of Justice in the case on genocide against the Rohingya in Myanmar. According to the Nobel Committee, Pillay shows "enormous courage" by committing herself to the prosecution of perpetrators of war crimes and crimes against humanity. Her work is of great significance for the international legal order, says the jury, which praises her "strong moral compass". Pillay was born into an Indian Tamil family during apartheid in South Africa. She became a lawyer and opposed the "deep-rooted structural discrimination, segregation and exclusion", according to the jury. Early in her career she defended Nelson Mandela and others who spoke out against apartheid. Importance of international law. Notably, the committee paid much attention to the importance of international law. "In a time of existential challenges, including more wars and conflicts than the world has known for a long time, international law is no longer merely a supplement to peace and security. It is an absolute necessity." That system of international law is currently "under enormous pressure", said the jury, "and its institutions are being attacked". "We see a shift towards power politics at the expense of legal frameworks and global respect for law and justice." And that is dangerous, the words of the jury make clear: "When might takes over from law, that undermines stability, trust and peaceful coexistence." The prize is therefore also a message to those who undermine international law, said the chair of the Nobel Committee. US President Trump recently attacked the ICC. He spoke of "show trials" and said he wants to "tear down the Court stone by stone". The US has already imposed sanctions on ICC staff and threatens even harsher sanctions. Benefiting from migration. On 9 June 2016 Pillay received an honorary doctorate from Erasmus University Rotterdam. At the time she gave the Mandeville Lecture, in which she spoke about human rights and the refugee crisis of that year. She observed then that xenophobia, rejection, suspicion and aggression were dominant in public debate. She said it was a misconception that migration would pose a threat. Europe had also benefited greatly from migration throughout its history, she argued. Nominations not known. The winner of the Nobel Prize is chosen each year by the Norwegian Nobel Committee. Members of that committee are Norwegian citizens selected by the Norwegian parliament for a term of six years. To be eligible for the prize, you must be nominated. According to news agency Reuters, US President Trump was nominated by Cambodia, Israel and Pakistan. Who else had a chance at the Peace Prize was not clear in advance. The full list of names is only made public after fifty years.

title: Netherlands Dachau Committee knew camp stories of 99-year-old were not true
lead: The Netherlands Dachau Committee has known since 2024 about the untruths regarding the wartime past of Willem Wilbrink and has tried to prevent him from spreading them further. That is what chairman <entity id="person:wimar-jaeger">Wimar Jaeger</entity> of the foundation told NOS. The 99-year-old Wilbrink was regularly at commemorations of the Second World War and at schools to talk about his wartime past and his time in the Dachau concentration camp. But a publication this week in Historisch Nieuwsblad shows that it is very unlikely he was ever imprisoned there. The publication also reveals that other claims he made are probably not true. By his own account, Wilbrink was arrested at the age of 15 for resistance work and taken to the concentration camp near Munich. There he is said to have been put to work as a corpse carrier. In that capacity he says he saved forty people from death. He did this, he claimed, by bringing people who were supposed to be dead and about to be put in the crematorium, but who turned out to be alive, to the infirmary. No evidence. According to researchers there is no evidence for these claims. For example, there is no documentation of his imprisonment in Dachau and no prisoner number is known for him, while in this concentration camp, where more than 43,000 people died, everything was recorded meticulously. Wilbrink also wears decorations of which it is unknown how he obtained them. For example, Wilbrink claimed he had received a Polish heroic title, but research by RTL Nieuws shows that his name does not appear in the country's archives, and that the title Wilbrink mentioned does not exist. Furthermore, Wilbrink told stories that other Dachau survivors had no memory of and which, according to researchers, also did not take place. Wilbrink also does not appear in the accounts of and about well-known people who were imprisoned in Dachau, such as those of priest and war hero Titus Brandsma, who was murdered there in 1942. Organisations informed about untruths. Jaeger says the National Dachau Committee discovered that Wilbrink's stories were not true after the publication of his biography. The organisation found that book remarkable because they did not know Wilbrink's story. The Committee therefore conducted research and spoke with historians, after which the conclusion was drawn that Wilbrink's past in Dachau was invented. "We then tried to stop the book from being distributed and informed commemoration committees that Wilbrink's story is not true", says Jaeger. The National Dachau Committee did not actively make the news about Wilbrink public because "we know better than anyone what a war trauma can do with the stories in your head", says chairman Jaeger. "We are convinced that Wilbrink thinks he experienced this." Jaeger states that the organisation has empathy and wants to understand people with war trauma, but also that it is important that stories about the Second World War and Dachau are based on the truth. Therefore the committee now cannot do anything but make clear what the reality is, he says. "Otherwise we have nothing to gain from the lessons we learned there." Although the Dachau committee already knew about the untruths in 2024, Wilbrink was still at the National Commemoration of the Capitulations 1945 in Wageningen in 2025. <entity id="person:vincent-karremans">Minister Karremans</entity> then wrote on LinkedIn that he "had the honour of sitting next to Wilbrink". The organisation of the Wageningen commemoration did not know about the untruths in the 99-year-old's story, a spokesperson says. He says Wageningen45 was not informed about this by the Netherlands Dachau Committee. According to him, the organisation relies on expert bodies when recognising veterans and their stories. "Wageningen45 has taken note of the Historisch Nieuwsblad article and takes this very seriously", he tells NOS. For the organisation, "it is paramount that the stories we tell and the change-makers we honour are reliable and authentic", the spokesperson says. "So that we can keep veterans' stories alive with great care and respect for a wide audience." Second World War newsletter Interested in the Second World War? Subscribe to our newsletter here.

title: A2 in Limburg closed all weekend, significant delays already this morning
lead: The A2 in Limburg will be completely closed in both directions this weekend. Last night the section between St. Joost and Roosteren was already closed. That was clearly noticeable during the morning rush hour: motorists faced significant delays. Tonight at 21.00 the A2 will close between junction Het Vonderen (Echt) and junction Kerensheide (Urmond) due to roadworks. The A2 is being widened: an extra lane will be added in both directions. The total works will last for years. This weekend <entity id="org:rijkswaterstaat">Rijkswaterstaat</entity> is running a liveblog about the so-called WeekendBreek . With such a full closure, work can continue day and night for a whole weekend. This weekend, among other things, two wildlife culverts are being built. Less traffic The first night of the works went smoothly despite the rain, Rijkswaterstaat tells L1 Nieuws. The motorway runs through the narrowest part of the Netherlands and there are no good alternative routes. Traffic today is being diverted from the St. Joost exit via Echt over the N276. Rijkswaterstaat urges people not to go on the road if it is not necessary. "There was somewhat less traffic heading north compared with other Fridays," said Rijkswaterstaat. Hundreds of people are working day and night on the A2 this weekend. It is the second weekend closure in a series of seven weekend closures over the next five years. The closure lasts until Monday morning at 05.00.

title: Thousands of Spaniards take to the streets to commemorate Maricarmen Abascal: 'This is murder'
lead: In Madrid, around twenty thousand people took to the streets last night to commemorate Maricarmen Abascal, who died on Wednesday. The 87-year-old woman became the face of large-scale housing protests after she was evicted by a real estate investor from the apartment where she had lived her entire adult life. The cause of the woman's death has not been disclosed, but since she was carried out of her home on a stretcher on 23 September, she had been in hospital with fear, stress and exhaustion. With many candles, flowers and cards with loving messages, the thousands of demonstrators last night marched from the Puerta del Sol, the central square of the Spanish capital, to her home in the prestigious Retiro neighbourhood. Anger at the property company. At the apartment complex, candles were lit and drawings and letters were placed, creating a makeshift altar. The demonstrators expressed their anger at the investment company that bought the residential building in 2020 and raised the woman's rent from 500 to more than 1600 euros per month. With her pension of 1400 euros, the woman could not pay this. The property manager then tried for years to get Abascal out of her home, but through all kinds of legal proceedings she managed to resist this. Until late September. The demonstrators chanted: "This is not a death, this is murder." One woman says: "This is about dignity." And: "Enough is enough. We cannot go on like this." A young man adds: "Maricarman's situation is not unique. She symbolises everything we fight for: a dignified existence now and in the future." The fact that after Abascal's eviction the property company gave way under massive public pressure and the woman was nonetheless allowed to return to her home, at a reduced rent, has not made the demonstrators any milder. Just a few hours before she was due to sign her new tenancy agreement, she died in the Gregorio Marañón hospital in Madrid. 'Maricarmen lives on'. "Drive these vultures out of our neighbourhoods", was chanted. A spokesperson for a tenants' union became emotional while reading out a tribute to the woman: "The struggle continues, Maricarmen lives on", she said. A minute's silence followed for the woman who became an icon in the fight against speculation and high house prices in Spain. Many Spaniards cannot afford a home because of inflation and a shortage of housing. Especially in Madrid, Barcelona and Valencia there is too little housing. Because of the social unrest, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez on Monday called early elections for 29 November.

title: Former OpenAI employees speak out about their dismissal and warn the company
lead: Three dismissed OpenAI employees warn the company in an open letter of a culture of fear. The three-page letter was published by them on social media. Last week the American company dismissed the three safety employees. According to OpenAI, they had shared company information with external parties. In the letter, the dismissed employees deny this. They think they were dismissed because they had voiced criticism and concerns internally about the safety of the AI models. The dismissal has since set off a rumour mill, as a result of which people who still work at OpenAI no longer dare to voice criticism. "If OpenAI employees no longer feel free to raise internal safety concerns, then we all run the risk of something catastrophic really going wrong", they write in the letter. They also call on OpenAI to work with an external regulator. OpenAI response A spokesperson for the company, responding to the open letter, told The Wallstreet Journal that the employees were not dismissed because they had criticised the company's safety measures. OpenAI also says it is grateful for the contributions the three former employees have made. OpenAI has been much in the news recently, because the company lost control of its own AI models. Within three months, OpenAI has had to halt its work twice. The first time was in July, when 1200 agents managed to break into the AI company Hugging Face.

title: Riots during large strike against cuts in Brussels
lead: In Brussels, a strike by trade unions has turned into disorder. Riots have broken out near Brussels-Central station. Streets are blocked and police are being pelted with fireworks, stones and bottles. Police are responding with tear gas. A water cannon has also been deployed. The demonstrators are protesting against the national government's policy of cutting social security spending. The government is currently deliberating over the budget. The protesters fear that wages, public services and pensions will also be cut. According to the trade unions, the strongest shoulders must bear the heaviest burdens. Black clothing Hundreds of young people dressed in black and wearing masks are, according to Belgian media, responsible for the unrest. They are said to have mixed in among the demonstrators. Several people have been arrested, but it is unclear how many. According to VRT, the trade union march is proceeding calmly in other parts of Brussels. Thousands of people are marching through the city. Because of the strike, a large part of public transport in Brussels has come to a standstill. There is also disruption at the airport. Watch footage of the disturbances here:

title: France warned about non-visible military aircraft near Curaçao
lead: France warned during the American attack on Venezuela on 3 January about military aircraft that were not visible to civil air traffic control in the Caribbean region. Because they were not visible, air traffic controllers could not always inform other aircraft about the presence of military aircraft. That is evident from documents that the Dutch <entity id="org:ministerie-van-buitenlandse-zaken">ministerie van Buitenlandse Zaken</entity> released following an appeal to the Open Government Act (Woo). NOS reported on 14 December already about a near-collision between a passenger aircraft and an American military tanker aircraft above Curaçao, in which the military aircraft was not visible on radar. The danger of military aircraft that are not visible to civil air traffic control is that air traffic controllers cannot warn other aircraft in time. Without information about the position of those aircraft, they also cannot ensure sufficient separation between aircraft. Pilots of passenger aircraft can therefore unexpectedly encounter a military aircraft and may then have to intervene themselves to prevent a collision. That risk also played a role in the near-collision NOS reported on in December. The French warning makes clear that during the American attack on Venezuela, military aircraft that stayed out of sight of civil air traffic controllers were again taken into account. Listen here to part of the conversation between air traffic control and the pilots during the near-collision: The French warning related to the flight information regions of Curaçao, San Juan and Piarco. Pilots were also advised to take extra fuel, within operational possibilities, so they could divert if necessary. The documents do not show that such aircraft actually flew in the Curaçao flight information region on 3 January. Emergency consultation after near-collision. The incidents NOS first reported on led to emergency consultation between airlines, the American aviation authority FAA, Curaçao air traffic control and international aviation organisations. KLM subsequently tightened its safety measures for flights through Curaçao airspace. Aircraft had to carry extra lighting throughout the entire flight through that area from then on. On 18 December, the governments of Curaçao and Aruba reported that agreements had been made with the United States about American military aircraft switching on transponders. American flight ban. Just over two weeks later came the American attacks on Venezuela, in which President Maduro and his wife were captured and taken to the United States. On 3 January the FAA issued a flight ban for American civil aviation operators in the Curaçao Flight Information Region (FIR). This applied at all flight levels due to safety risks from military activities. American military and state aircraft were exempt from the ban. The Curaçao FIR covers a large part of the southern Caribbean and borders the Venezuelan flight information region Maiquetía. Air traffic services are provided by Curaçao air traffic control. The American ban applied to American aviation operators and did not mean that airspace was closed for all aircraft. Other airlines had to assess for themselves whether they could operate their flights safely. See our special on the near-collision here: KLM cancelled flights to the ABC islands, Sint Maarten and several other Caribbean destinations on 3 January. TUI and Corendon also cancelled flights. According to Buitenlandse Zaken, around 2600 KLM passengers were affected by the cancellations. The Curaçao <entity id="org:regering">regering</entity> said at the time that the airspace was not completely closed, but that there was heightened readiness. Airlines had to assess for themselves whether they could fly. On 4 January the American restrictions were lifted and airlines resumed their flights to the islands. Crisis consultation in The Hague. The Dutch government held crisis consultation on 3 January about the American attacks and the consequences for the region. Among those involved were the ministries of Buitenlandse Zaken, <entity id="org:ministerie-van-defensie">Defensie</entity>, <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-biza">Binnenlandse Zaken</entity>, <entity id="org:ministerie-van-infrastructuur-en-waterstaat">Infrastructuur en Waterstaat</entity> and <entity id="org:ministerie-van-justitie-en-veiligheid">Justitie en Veiligheid</entity>. Representatives of KLM, TUI fly and Corendon also received information about the security situation. On 4 January it was announced that a steering group for the Caribbean region, chaired by Binnenlandse Zaken, would convene. Defensie and Buitenlandse Zaken would share information there. The released documents do not show when the Curaçao aviation authorities were informed about the international security warnings, or which agreements were made with the United States about military flight movements during the attack. Crisis phase scaled down. On 6 January the Dutch crisis consultation convened again. The consultation decided to return the crisis approach to the pre-crisis phase. A next consultation was planned for 13 January, unless the situation gave cause to convene earlier. The scenario analyses on which the decision-making was partly based have been largely redacted. The documents made public do not state what information the Curaçao air traffic control had about military aircraft movements during the American attack. It also remains unclear whether the agreements that Curaçao and Aruba announced in December with the United States about the use of transponders during the operation were still in force and were being observed.

title: Rotterdam files a police report against employees for fraud in connection with the childcare benefits scandal
lead: The municipality of Rotterdam suspects that several employees committed fraud with money meant for victims of the childcare benefits scandal. The municipality has filed a police report against two people, the regional broadcaster Rijnmond reports. Five others have been put on leave. The municipality is still investigating them. The employees helped victims of the childcare benefits scandal, for example with buying new furniture or equipment at the municipality's expense. They had access to a municipal payment card for this. The victims received help from the municipality because they had run into financial problems after the <entity id="org:belastingdienst">Belastingdienst</entity> wrongly accused them of fraud with childcare benefit. Spending for themselves The municipality of Rotterdam believes that at least two civil servants also bought items for themselves or others. These concern expenses where it is not clear what the money was spent on, and expenses where it is not clear why they were made. "As far as we know, the victims simply received their items. They did not lose out, but that does not change the fact that it is fraud," says alderman Diederik van Dommelen (VVD) to Rijnmond. The possible fraud was discovered more than a year ago following a report about one of the employees. A hundred people Van Dommelen does not yet know how much money is involved. That is currently being investigated. "What happened is truly unacceptable. I want to know what happened and how much went wrong." Around a hundred people had access to the municipality's credit card. The alderman considers it justifiable that so many people had the freedom to make purchases for the victims. "Let's not forget: we did this to help the victims, and then you need speed, because those people need help," he says. "Speed and care sometimes clash." To prevent fraud, the spending limits have since been adjusted. "We have also reduced the number of people who can use the credit card," said alderman Van Dommelen. Fingers in the sugar bowl "We cannot prevent people from having their fingers in the sugar bowl. But we must be able to detect it as quickly as possible," said the alderman. "The checks therefore need to be faster. At the same time, we want to be able to help the victims quickly. It will always be a search for balance."

title: Renoir paintings found a month after theft from French museum
lead: Two Renoir paintings stolen last month from a museum in southern France have been found. The police do not want to say where they were found or whether they are damaged. The works concerned are Madame Colonna Romano and Jeune Femme au puits, which were stolen. On 8 September, four paintings by the well-known French impressionist Pierre-Auguste Renoir were stolen from the Musée Renoir in Cagnes-sur-Mer. The value of the four works is estimated at 9 million euros. Within three minutes the thieves managed to get in, take the canvases and leave unseen. During their escape outside, two thieves left two paintings behind in the museum garden. Six arrests On Wednesday six suspects were arrested, including the two suspected burglars. The six are, among other things, suspected of theft in an organised context. The paintings are normally on display at the Musée d'Orsay in Paris, but were on loan. The four pieces were the most valuable works of the Musée Renoir. The museum is located in the painter's last home.

title: Hobby fishers also deployed to remove harmful crayfish
lead: Hobby fishers, sport fishing clubs, contractors and muskrat control officers may in future also catch invasive American crayfish on a larger scale. Currently the water boards do this, but they do not have enough people to push back the harmful crayfish population. So a new regulation for fishing invasive crayfish is coming, <entity id="person:silvio-erkens">staatssecretaris Erkens</entity> told <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity> today. Tunnels and burrows In Dutch ditches, canals, lakes and pools an estimated tens of millions of crayfish are causing major damage to water quality and biodiversity. They cut water plants to pieces with their claws, eat aquatic insects and amphibian and fish eggs. They also dig tunnels and burrows, making banks and dikes less stable. The invasive crayfish reproduce quickly and it is no longer possible to remove the animals completely. But the ministry does want to do more about the so-called 'catching away' of the animals. Umbrella trap So other catching equipment may now be used, such as the slot trap and the umbrella trap. Currently the water boards mainly work with fyke nets and cubs, but the drawback is that many other fish and aquatic animals are caught too. These are then returned, but are often injured or have already died from the catch. Hiring in other fishers, such as sport fishers, members of fishing clubs, contractors and muskrat control officers is also new. Until now they were only allowed to catch crayfish on a small scale, namely with a rod. Under the new rules more is allowed, but that does not mean everyone may always catch crayfish. A water board can locally put out "an assignment", says state secretary Erkens (Fisheries), and hobby fishers, for example, can then get to work on it. Crayfish cuisine Erkens speaks of "an important step" to bring the plague under control. He does point out that once caught, the animals must not be released elsewhere. "They must be destroyed or consumed." The state secretary himself has eaten crayfish before, he says when asked. "I found them quite tasty," said Erkens. "Who knows, a very nice Dutch crayfish cuisine may be on the verge of emerging." Ruben Ariaans is a professional crayfish fisher. He is not really keen on hobby fishers also going hunting for the animal:

title: Twenty asylum seekers slept in the rain in Ter Apel: 'Fallen below the humane minimum'
lead: In Ter Apel, twenty people who want to apply for asylum slept outside on the grass in the rain last night. According to the aid organisations Vluchtelingenwerk Nederland and the Red Cross, this is a direct result of the lack of reception places in the Netherlands. According to the aid organisations, the Netherlands is falling below a "humane minimum". At the registration centre in Ter Apel there is a building with day shelter. There is room there for a maximum of 150 people. People who want to apply for asylum can go there if there is no place at the registration centre. "We now have people who have been in that shelter for ten days, people cannot wash there", says a spokesperson for the Red Cross to NOS. The limit of 150 people has been reached several times in recent weeks, the aid organisations say.
