NOS correspondents Kysia Hekster (NATO) and Christiaan Paauwe (Central and Eastern Europe) explain in the stream what makes the speech so special. "Do you have a place to stay?" asks an aid worker. On her phone she notes the details of Vidmantas (61), who is sitting opposite her in the white reception tent. "No, I have nowhere to go," answers the 'refugee'. On the green grass field of the racecourse in Lazdijai, a Lithuanian town close to the border with Poland, so-called displaced Lithuanians are being shown around. Vidmantas is one of the hundreds of citizens taking part. He wants to know what happens in an "extreme situation", he says after he has registered. "So that you don't get confused when it happens." After registration, participants can receive psychological or medical help in other tents, or something to eat. A large Lithuanian flag hangs from a crane above the 'refugee camp'. Further on, green tents with camp beds are set up in rows. Weak points The scenario is that the eastern border area of Lithuania threatens to be invaded and a stream of refugees gets under way. Captain Darius Indrisonis of the fire brigade sounds almost enthusiastic when giving a tour. According to him, they can learn a lot from the exercise and see where the weak points are. For example, it turned out that registration was too slow and many people had to wait. That Lithuania is going this far with preparations is characteristic of how the threat is felt on NATO's eastern flank. The country has had a lot to deal with in recent years in terms of sabotage attacks and other incidents. A few weeks ago, a drone that flew in from Belarus was shot down over Lithuania. Backpacks already packed Kristupas (17) and Gabriele (19) receive a first aid demonstration in a tent. Due to all the siren tests, the drones flying in and the military actions, the young couple notices tension is rising in Lithuania. "Taken together, you feel it is getting more and more serious," says Kristupas. They have already made some preparations in case war breaks out, Gabriele says. For example, they have an escape plan and packed backpacks. In recent weeks, European leaders and intelligence services have repeatedly warned that Russia is intent on further escalation. For example, new barracks are being built on the Russian side of the border. 'Want to be prepared' Does the Lithuanian government therefore take into account that Moscow may not be deterred by NATO and could start a direct war? "We see no indication that we need to be ready next month or the month after," says Tomas Daukantas, the chancellor of the Lithuanian government, to NOS. "But we do want to be prepared. Then we have every confidence that we can handle it." Still, for some the exercise is mainly an outing. A 56-year-old woman from the area watches with her two grandchildren as 'victims' receive first aid. She does not expect such a refugee camp will ever be needed. The 17-year-old Kristupas does not assume the worst-case scenario either. But the war threat does affect his future plans. He is in the last year of secondary school and wants to study medicine in Kaunas, where his girlfriend Gabriele already is. "You do ask yourself: which city would be safe? Should I look abroad too?"

title: No delivery and wrong shop prices after 'cyber security incident' at Albert Heijn
lead: Albert Heijn, Etos and Gall & Gall have been experiencing a disruption since Sunday afternoon. According to Ahold Delhaize , the parent company of Albert Heijn, this is due to a "cyber security incident". Albert Heijn earlier wrote in its own press release about "an IT incident". Websites, apps and the customer service of Albert Heijn are unavailable due to the technical problems. Online ordered groceries also cannot be delivered, and electronic shelf labels still show last week's promotional prices instead of the current prices. The loyalty systems are not working either. The Belgian supermarket chain Delhaize, part of the same company as Albert Heijn, is also experiencing problems, reports VRT Nieuws . Customers cannot place new orders there for this week, and the customer service is also unreachable. In Belgium the app and website are accessible. Protecting data: It is still unclear what exactly is going on. Albert Heijn does not want to say anything about this. "We have immediately taken measures to protect our IT environment. Part of that is the preventive temporary shutdown of a number of systems", Albert Heijn writes in a statement. "We are investigating the incident and working on restoring our services. Protecting the data of our customers, employees and partners is paramount", the supermarket chain reports. The Albert Heijn stores opened as usual this morning. The supermarket chain says it does not yet know when the services will be available again. This Albert Heijn branch in Amsterdam informs customers with a note about the incorrect prices in the store:

title: Bricks without gas kilns? Full power grid stands in the way of more sustainable industry
lead: Many regional industrial companies cannot make their operations more sustainable. For the production of glass, cardboard and stone, for example, they often use large machines that consume a lot of energy. In the coming years these must be replaced, and companies would preferably do so by switching to electric machines. But there is too little room on the power grid. That is stated in the report by Cluster6, a partnership of regional energy-intensive industrial companies in manufacturing, waste processing and the Ministry of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-kgg">Klimaat en Groene Groei</entity>. The brickworks of the company Wienerberger are also affiliated with the partnership. Some 70 million bricks and paving stones are made there each year, still largely with the help of gas kilns. But if it is up to director Jasper Vos, those will quickly become electric appliances. One of the factories is on the waiting list for a heavier power connection. "We were promised that there would be room somewhere before 2030, but the question is whether that will actually happen," he says at the location in Pannerden, north-east of Nijmegen. Grid congestion First of all, why is there not enough capacity on the power grid? That is because in recent years companies and households have switched to electricity to a great extent, but the underground cables were not designed for that. This creates grid congestion; in the morning and evening demand for power is much higher than during the day and at night. The grid operator takes these 'peaks' into account and therefore cannot grant every new request. In any case, not before the cables can handle it. Therefore grid operators are reinforcing the power grid. The Netherlands Authority for Consumers and Markets introduced measures two years ago to resolve shortages on the power grid. This means that socially important institutions such as schools and hospitals get priority on the grid. Companies that help reduce grid congestion, such as solar and wind parks or companies installing large batteries, also get priority on the waiting list. Industrial companies end up at the very bottom of the waiting list. Interim solutions Because the waiting list is tied to a region, companies in a region where there is little 'competition' on the power grid may get a connection immediately, while companies elsewhere have to wait for years. "Take for example a glass factory that wants to become sustainable in 2030. If the grid operator tells it that there is only room in 2034, the factory has to bridge that gap," says Barbara Verwayen, who represents the regional industrial companies on behalf of Cluster6. According to her, temporary, local generation of electricity at the companies could offer an interim solution. "If that can be done sustainably, then that is terrific, with sun, wind and batteries. If it cannot be done sustainably, we will have to temporarily generate extra electricity with gas turbines." In this way companies could, while waiting for a heavier power connection, still start investing in electric machines. But more is needed for that than money alone, says Verwayen. "Laws and regulations, the legal framework, granting of permits, all those things." Resistance Grid operators have been working on reinforcing the power grid for some time. To do so, they are building around a hundred high-voltage stations and other power infrastructure in the coming years. Finding a suitable location is often complicated. Protected flora and fauna or proximity to a Natura 2000 area can make building a new station impossible. In addition, operators often encounter resistance from local residents who would rather not see an industrial high-voltage station in their 'backyard'. This causes delays and uncertainty about the expansion of the power grid in the Netherlands. "Due to uncertainty about a power connection, investments are leaking away abroad," says Vos of the Wienerberger brickworks. "You look over the river here to Germany. Similar companies in neighbouring countries do have access to electricity. If we do not get that certainty and space, the survival of this type of company in the Netherlands is at stake."

title: Strike in Belgium over cuts to public services: fewer trains, VRT also on strike
lead: In Belgium, trade unions are protesting again today against announced cuts by <entity id="org:regering">de regering</entity>. The strike day will affect schools, public transport and waste collection. Staff at the Flemish broadcaster VRT are also laying down their work. The strike is an initiative of the socialist union ACOD. The protest is aimed at the cuts to public services announced by the regering-De Wever. Tomorrow the prime minister was due to explain the budget choices in his State of the Union, but due to the absence of a budget agreement that has been postponed. His government has been in crisis since this weekend, because the coalition parties cannot agree on that budget. Rail: The strike at the Belgian railway company NMBS began yesterday evening and until 10.00 p.m. this evening fewer trains will run. This also affects train travel to and from the Netherlands, NS reports. Travellers are advised to check the journey planner before departure. Fewer buses, trams and metros are also running in Belgium. Staff at broadcaster VRT are also laying down their work. The broadcaster still has to cut 10 million euros, on top of an earlier announced round of cuts. Many TV broadcasts are being scrapped, news bulletins have been shortened and on the radio there will mostly be music, the broadcaster reports. On 9 November a decision will be taken on further actions. Riots: Last Friday a strike in Brussels against cuts to social security ended in riots, after hundreds to thousands of masked youths had mixed in among the demonstrators. They threw stones and fireworks at the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity>. The police said the disturbances were not linked to the union action. At least 110 people were arrested. A day earlier a ban on gatherings was announced in Liège, because of education protests that had got out of hand in that city. Those protests have partly spilled over from France, where since last month demonstrations have been held against, among other things, the poor state of school buildings and the teacher shortage.

title: Centre-left puts Raphaël Glucksmann forward as French presidential candidate
lead: With a comfortable win in the primaries, Raphaël Glucksmann will become the candidate of the centre-left bloc in next year's French elections. The 46-year-old member of the European Parliament must unite the fragmented left camp as presidential candidate. Glucksmann won 66 percent of the more than 120,000 online votes last night, so a second round was not needed. The leader of Place Publique (PP) finished well ahead of Olivier Faure of Parti Socialiste (PS), who got only 14.5 percent of the votes. The chance that Glucksmann, essayist and son of philosopher André Glucksmann , becomes president is small. That is because radical-left politician Jean-Luc Mélenchon of La France Insoumise (LFI) refuses to rally behind a joint left-wing candidate and thereby keeps the division within the left in place. Hollande's participation Glucksmann founded his party Place Publique in 2018 as a pro-European and social-democratic alternative to the PS of former president François Hollande. In the European Parliament he represents both Place Publique and the PS. There, among other things, he campaigned hard for the position of the Uyghurs in China. There are also politicians who did not take part in the centre-left primaries. The most notable is the 72-year-old former president François Hollande, who may possibly make another bid for the presidency outside the primaries. Bag of flour Glucksmann celebrated his win last night afterwards in a bar in Paris. As he walked to a taxi afterwards, someone threw a bag of flour over his head, French media write. An attack with a bag of flour also befell Jordan Bardella, party leader of the radical-right party Rassemblement National (RN), in November 2025. He immediately expressed his support for Glucksmann on X and condemned the incident as "unacceptable violence". According to him, there is no such thing as a small attack. "Every physical attack is serious." On French television, after the primaries, Glucksmann presented himself as the candidate who stands for a "break with Macronism", a "break with Mélenchon's hegemony over the left" and as "the candidate who can defeat our long-standing enemy, the far right". Support among young people The radical-right Marine Le Pen currently stands the best in the polls. According to a recent poll, she gets between 33 and 35 percent of the votes in the first round of the presidential election. According to various polls, Mélenchon is a possible candidate who would have to face Le Pen in the second round. The LFI leader has a lot of support among young French voters. Yesterday, during a campaign rally, he still called for lowering the voting age to 16 and for abolishing selective admission to universities. Glucksmann also expressed his support yesterday for pupils who have massively taken to the streets over the past few weeks . "They are asking for simple things: a teacher in the classroom and education in school buildings that are not dilapidated or unhealthy. They can count on me." Two terms That more than 120,000 eligible French voters took part in the online vote for the centre-left primary is a lot, but still considerably less than in earlier socialist primaries. The socialist primaries in 2011, which were won by the later president Hollande, drew 2.8 million participants. The three other centre-left candidates, Ségolène Royal, Jérôme Guedj and Emmanuel Maurel, each received less than 10 percent of the votes. Although Glucksmann opposes Macron's liberal positions on business, he, like the French president, supports further European cooperation and support for Ukraine. The French elections take place next year on 18 April (first round) and 2 May (second round). President Macron may not stand for re-election after two terms of office and ten years as president.

title: Oldest covered market in Paris destroyed by fire
lead: A large fire in the centre of Paris has destroyed the Marché des Enfants Rouges. The market was the oldest covered market in Paris. How the fire started is still unclear. The fire raged overnight. To extinguish it, 150 firefighters and around fifty fire engines were deployed. Firefighters told the Parisian newspaper Le Parisien that 1000 square metres were destroyed by the fire. The metal roof structure has also almost completely collapsed. Nothing remains of the covered market. No dead or injured. The market in the third arrondissement of Paris was popular among Parisians and tourists. The mayor of the arrondissement, Ariel Weil, was at the site where the market stood early this morning. "The shopkeepers are devastated. The good news is that there are no dead or injured." Buildings in the surroundings were also not damaged. According to the market's director, about twenty traders have been affected. Red children. The Marché des Enfants Rouges was built in 1615 on the orders of King Louis XIII and was the oldest covered market in Paris still in operation. In the 17th century the market had to meet the needs of the rapidly growing Le Marais district. The name of the market means "market of the red children", a reference to the nearby orphanage Hospice des Enfants-Rouges, where the children wore red clothing. When the orphanage closed its doors in 1772, the market was named after the 'red children'. Protest against closure. When the municipality had plans in 1994 to build an underground car park and extra homes, the market was threatened, but thanks to an action by, among others, local residents and politicians, the market was spared. An owner of an organic fruit and vegetable stall at the market reacts in Le Parisien, devastated. "I grew up there. It is very hard for me to see about 30 years of history go up in smoke."

title: Crash between crane and bus causes havoc in Nijmegen
lead: In Nijmegen a bus was damaged this morning in an accident with a crane truck. A passenger was injured and taken to hospital, Omroep Gelderland reports. The accident happened this morning around 07.00 hours on the Industrieweg, on the western edge of Nijmegen. While braking for a roundabout, the ballast of a crane truck hit the side of a bus carrying passengers. An advertising column and several lampposts along the road were also struck. Several emergency services, including several officers and an ambulance, went to the scene. A bus passenger who was sitting at the back of the bus was taken to hospital by ambulance staff. The other passengers were transported to Nijmegen by smaller buses. Havoc The collision caused havoc. A large part of the Industrieweg towards the centre of Nijmegen is strewn with debris from the advertising column, lampposts and glass. The <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> is investigating the cause.

title: SPD leader Bas steps down after attacks from coalition partner CDU in 'difficult time'
lead: Bärbel Bas, co-chair of the German governing party SPD, has unexpectedly stepped down. She also gives up her post as minister of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-sociale-zaken-en-werkgelegenheid">Sociale Zaken en Werkgelegenheid</entity>. The departure follows a death in the family and ongoing attacks on her personally. "After the death of my stepdaughter I realised I need more time to process the grief", Bas writes in a statement. Precisely in this "personally difficult time" the attacks on her have increased, she continues. "Also from the ranks of our coalition partner." According to the other co-chair, vice chancellor Lars Klingbeil, boundaries have been crossed. The attacks are "unseemly" and "poison the political culture", he says. "I am worried that we are losing empathetic figures in politics." Women in particular are targets of such attacks, hatred and incitement, according to Klingbeil. Bas belonged to the heart of the German government, but as minister repeatedly clashed with federal chancellor Merz and his CDU/CSU. The Christian Democrats want to reduce social contributions and regularly came up against Bas, who belongs to the left wing of the social democratic SPD. When Merz claimed that the current welfare state is unsustainable, Bas spoke of "bullshit". In recent weeks the CDU/CSU criticised Bas for the slow implementation of controversial pension plans, which are unpopular within the SPD. Bas would have deliberately slowed the reforms, while it was known within the coalition that there was a death in her family. Sour relationship The attacks on Bas are heavily criticised by SPD members. "The attacks by the CDU, despite her personally difficult situation, were inhumane and reckless", writes the influential SPD member Manuela Schwesig, state premier of Mecklenburg-Voor-Pommeren. Party colleague Bernd Rützel speaks of unacceptable attacks, both by CDU members and by "certain media". Within the CDU/CSU, Bas's outburst is in fact seen as inappropriate. Focus Online writes that the parliamentary group stayed away from criticism precisely because of her situation. An insider told the news site it was a "cheap kick when she is down". According to the Süddeutsche Zeitung, Merz did complain about Bas's absence, including to journalists. It shows how sour the relationship between the governing parties has become. Both parties feel the other is obstructing agreed reforms. Merz recently blocked the planned sugar tax, a project of SPD vice chancellor Klingbeil. On the other side, the SPD has objections to pension reforms. The election of a parliamentary president from the radical right-wing AfD in the state of Saksen-Anhalt, with the help of CDU votes, also led to tension. The SPD demands an explanation of this and wants the coalition partner to act against those who voted for it. Conversely, the CDU is pressuring the SPD not to govern with Die Linke in the state of Berlin, a party that the Christian Democrats consider antisemitic. Negotiations on healthcare reforms became so tense that federal president Steinmeier had to intervene, because he feared the government would collapse. Both parties, however, have no interest in a coalition break-up or new elections. The CDU/CSU in particular has fallen into free fall in the polls in recent weeks. Merz critic as successor Bas's ministerial post will be taken over by Alexander Schweitzer, former premier of the state of <entity id="org:waterschap-van-rijnland">Rijnland</entity>-Palts. In the past week he openly criticised Merz, who "does not deliver" and governs with a "cold neoliberal spirit of the 1990s". He also sneered that the CDU does not convincingly support Merz. With Schweitzer in this important post, the government once again has an SPD member who takes a critical stance towards the CDU's reform plans. At the same time there is little room to tinker with the agreements already concluded. It is now up to federal chancellor Merz to keep the squabbling coalition together. After the defeats in recent state elections, there was much speculation about his resignation. He stayed on, but with diminished authority within the party. He has tied his fate to carrying out the reforms. The party leadership met today to discuss how the CDU should proceed. Later today Merz will hold a press conference on this.

title: Dismissed dentist drives into dental practice in Belgium out of revenge
lead: In Belgium a dismissed dentist drove his car into a dental practice out of revenge. The driver was slightly injured. He was taken in by police for questioning. According to the Flemish broadcaster VRT, the Romanian man drove his Porsche through the rear of the building in Stekene in East Flanders at around 22.30 hours last night. The driver drove through the glass entrance door of the waiting room, put the car in reverse and then drove into the practice once more. The rear of the building was badly damaged. It took hours for the fire brigade to clear the damage and close the windows and doors. VRT reports that the man worked at the practice but had been dismissed. Nothing has been made public about the reason for his dismissal.

title: Cabinet wants to make it easier for zoos to improve enclosures
lead: There must be new rules for zoos, believes <entity id="person:silvio-erkens">staatssecretaris Erkens</entity> of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-landbouw-visserij-voedselzekerheid-en-natuur">Landbouw, Visserij, Voedselzekerheid en Natuur</entity>. Zoos that want to renew now face too many extra rules and permits, he believes. Whereas zoos that leave everything as it is have no trouble at all, precisely because they do not innovate. "Zoos have been a beloved outing for young and old for ages", writes Erkens in a letter to <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity>. "At the same time, over the years we have come to attach more value to animal welfare. It is therefore important that zoos keep up with the times." At the moment zoos still have permits for an indefinite period. Only zoos that want to innovate face new tests and the associated costs. A zoo that never changes anything can go on for years without running into rules. Erkens wants to change that. No flexibility Animal care manager Tjerk ter Meulen of zoo Artis in Amsterdam cites as an example the stones in an aquarium. For a permit application, all of them must be marked on a floor plan, including size and weight, he says. "That gives us no flexibility to change them again when the fish need it. Of course we want to constantly respond to the needs and welfare of the animals. And if we then have to apply for a new permit for the enclosure every time, that of course makes things very difficult."

title: Cyberattack hits French supermarkets, cooling systems set to 50 degrees
lead: Several French supermarket chains have been hit by a cyberattack. Hackers have disrupted cooling systems in supermarkets. Instead of cooling, they gave off heat; some systems had been set to 50 degrees above zero. Numerous supermarkets have had to throw away their stock. Hundreds of stores across France have been affected. These include branches of, among others, Intermarché, E.Leclerc, Netto and Coopérative U. Those stores had cooling equipment from a Danish manufacturer. Hackers got in via outdated software on those devices. The director of Coopérative U calls the attack unprecedented and extremely serious. Tropical levels The cyberattack happened last night. As a result, it only became clear what had happened at opening time. By then the mercury in some cold rooms and freezer compartments had already risen to tropical levels. An owner of one store in Alsace tells French media that the damage there is 220,000 euros. Nationally, the damage is almost certainly in the many millions. The companies have not yet named any amounts themselves. Urgent consultations were held this morning between the supermarkets and the supplier of the cooling equipment. Other companies were also involved. The French National Cybersecurity Agency is in contact with the software supplier and is investigating whether more companies have been affected by the attack. Incident in the Netherlands too The cyberattack on French supermarkets coincides with a "cyber security incident" at Albert Heijn in the Netherlands . That affects stores of Albert Heijn, Etos and Gall & Gall. This does not involve cooling systems, but among other things the electronic price tags on the shelves. Groceries ordered online cannot be delivered. Belgian Delhaize stores are also experiencing problems from the incident, as parent company Ahold Delhaize calls it. So it is not just a glitch. A spokesperson for Ahold Delhaize tells news agency Reuters that there is no reason to see a link between the two cyber incidents.

title: Podcast De Dag: Trump versus the International Criminal Court
lead: The American president Trump has been attacking the International Criminal Court for some time. On Friday he added a new chapter to that: the government announced new sanctions that are to apply to the entire court. In six months, working with or through American companies will be made impossible, which will affect almost everything at the Court. The attacks from the US are not new; Americans have considered the court unnecessary from the start. Listen here: You can listen to this episode of De Dag via NPO Luister and all other podcast apps. Like it? Then don't forget to subscribe. Journalist Stephanie van den Berg follows the International Criminal Court for news agency Reuters and says there is even discussion about whether you will still be able to buy coffee at the court. If the sanctions take effect, judges can always fall back on old-fashioned printing, for example if documents may no longer be stored on American servers. European politicians want to change the Americans' minds in the coming months, but how? Reactions: email to dedag@nos.nl Presentation & editing: Marco Geijtenbeek Editor: IJsbrand Terpstra

title: Escalation looms in the Middle East: five questions about Saudi Arabia and the Houthis
lead: The international airport in the Saudi capital Riyad came under fire several times last week by the Houthis from Yemen, resulting in deaths. In the heaviest attack, on Saturday, thirteen people were killed and more than three hundred were injured. A day later another death occurred at the airport. The Houthis are not targeting just any airport: King Khalid International Airport is a busy hub in the Middle East and handles around 800 flights a day. Five questions about the attacks. What do the Houthi attacks on Riyad airport mean? It is a further escalation of the war in the Middle East. The direct hit is the deadliest attack on Saudi territory in more than ten years. The Saudis have vowed to strike back hard. The Houthis made important territorial gains along the Red Sea in September. Among other things, they captured the port city of Mokka and the strategic island of Perim in the Bab al-Mandab strait. Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government army then started a counteroffensive. The Yemeni government now says it has regained control of the strait, but fighting is still ongoing. The Houthis see the attacks on Riyad as retaliatory actions within the conflict currently taking place around the Red Sea. The moment on Saturday when a missile hits Riyad airport: Why do the Saudis support the Yemeni government army? Saudi Arabia has for years regarded the Houthis as a threat to its security. The movement controls large parts of the north of Yemen, on Saudi Arabia's southern border, and has repeatedly fired missiles and drones into Saudi territory. On top of that comes the regional power struggle between the rivals Saudi Arabia and Iran. The Houthis are allies of Iran and share the same opponents: the US, Israel and Saudi Arabia. Iran has for years supplied the Houthis with weapons and missile technology. As a result, the Houthis have grown into an important ally of Iran in the region. By choosing Iran's side, they hope to strengthen their own position relative to the Saudi kingdom. Saudi Arabia has therefore supported the internationally recognised Yemeni government in the fight against the Houthis since 2015. The movement's recent territorial gains around the Bab al-Mandab strait make that fight even more important for Riyad. The strait is a crucial route for international trade and Saudi oil exports, especially now that shipping through the Strait of Hormuz is being hindered. Who are the Houthis? We explain that and four other questions in this article. What is the aim of the Houthis? The Houthis primarily want to maintain and strengthen their power in Yemen. At the same time they are trying to grow into a player that both the United States and Saudi Arabia must take into account. The Houthis have in recent years become increasingly skilled at perfecting missiles and evading Patriot air defence systems. With their attacks on Saudi airports they show that they can also cause major damage outside Yemen. The Houthis are fighting on two fronts: against Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones on one side, and in Yemen against the government army. How will this continue? For now, an end to the violence does not appear to be in sight. Saudi Arabia has announced it will strike back hard and is already carrying out attacks on Houthi targets in Yemen. The Houthis in turn threaten new attacks on Saudi airports and other important infrastructure. In addition, the US may get involved. President Trump has not ruled out military support for Saudi Arabia. Washington has also sent extra warships and soldiers to the Middle East. The stakes for the world economy are high. If the Houthis further disrupt shipping in the Bab al-Mandab, a second important trade route, alongside the Strait of Hormuz, comes under pressure. That could push oil prices up further. At the same time, Trump is cautious about a new major military operation. The war he is waging against Iran is extremely unpopular in the US, and there are mid-term elections in three weeks. What else does this escalation say about the war in the Middle East? The fighting in Yemen shows how difficult it is to confine the war between the US, Israel and Iran to a single front. Regional allies and opponents are becoming increasingly involved in the conflict. Iran has not completely lost its power position despite months of American and Israeli attacks. With support from allies such as the Houthis, Tehran can continue to exert pressure on important trade routes and American allies in the region. For the Americans that is a problem. Despite their military superiority, they have not succeeded in removing the threat from Iran and its allies. The attacks on Saudi Arabia show that the war can spread quickly and further, with all the consequences that entails for regional security and the world economy.

title: Misconduct reported at Utrecht nursing home: 'She simply hasn't been showered for a year'
lead: Relatives of residents of a care centre in <entity id="org:gemeente-utrecht">Utrecht</entity> sound the alarm with RTV Utrecht about the conditions on a nursing ward. They say residents are poorly cared for and often left to their own devices. The psychogeriatric ward of Nieuw Tamarinde in Overvecht houses around twenty elderly people who have some form of dementia. Nieuw Tamarinde is part of care institution Careyn. It is active in the municipalities of <entity id="org:gemeente-stichtse-vecht">Stichtse Vecht</entity>, <entity id="org:gemeente-de-ronde-venen">De Ronde Venen</entity>, <entity id="org:gemeente-woerden">Woerden</entity>, <entity id="org:gemeente-oudewater">Oudewater</entity>, <entity id="org:gemeente-montfoort">Montfoort</entity>, Utrecht and Zeist. RTV Utrecht spoke with several relatives of residents, who wish to remain anonymous. They describe the problems that are occurring on the ward. For example, there is said to be poor care, a lack of hygiene and problems with administering medication. According to the relatives, staff are often nowhere to be seen. 'Not showered for a year' Two women describe the lack of care for their aunt: "She stank at one point. Her nails were very long and there was faeces under them. She was wearing dirty clothes, greasy hair and no mouth care had been done." RTV Utrecht has viewed the aunt's file. Staff members write in it how the woman is doing and what they have done. For example, a carer writes on 4 May this year that "madam" has not been showered for a year because she "resists". The plan is now to wash the woman with two people from now on, so that she can resist less. "She simply hasn't been showered for a year," says her niece indignantly. "She would not have wanted that." 'My mother's dentures were stuck fast' Another woman describes the situation with her husband. "I went there every day. At 9.30 he would be sitting in his wheelchair with greasy hair and black nails," she says. "Then they would pay attention to it and then it would go well for a while." According to a fourth woman, her mother's dentures are not being cleaned. "Her dentures were stuck fast," she says. She describes how a staff member forcefully pulled the dentures out of her mother's mouth. "Her dentures hadn't come out for months." Temporary agency staff The relatives have complained several times to Careyn's management, but so far, they state, little has changed. "It goes well for a bit when you say something about it, and then it's wrong again," says one of them. Careyn's management acknowledges the problems and attributes them to staff shortages. In a complaints mediator's report it can be read: "Every time people drop out again, which partly undoes the improvements." Many temporary agency workers work on the ward, and according to the relatives that is where the problem lies. "A number of permanent staff are really very kind and good, but they are often not there," says a relative. Inspection reports Care institution Careyn informs RTV Utrecht in a written response that it is aware of the relatives' concerns and says it has taken measures to improve the situation. "We have also organised family evenings to listen to what is going on, to discuss concerns and to look together at what needs to be better." The care institution acknowledges that "things have not gone well". "The measures we have put in place have not yet led to the improvement that is needed on all points. We must also face that." The <entity id="org:inspectie-gezondheidszorg-en-jeugd">Inspectie Gezondheidszorg en Jeugd</entity> tells RTV Utrecht that seven reports have been received since the beginning of 2025. The inspectorate cannot say anything about the content of the reports or who made them. The inspectorate does not want to say whether an investigation into the ward will follow.

title: Albert Heijn distribution centers at a standstill after digital security incident, risk of empty shelves
lead: Work has come to a standstill at several Albert Heijn distribution centers as a result of the online security incident at the supermarket chain. This affects the supply of the stores, says CEO Margaret Versteden-van Duijn to NOS. Empty shelves may appear, especially for fresh products. "It is true that work has completely stopped at some distribution centers, because we had to shut down the systems as a precaution", she says. Albert Heijn has seven large distribution centers in the Netherlands. Versteden-Van Duijn does not want to say which of them are still operational. Albert Heijn expects that shelf-stable products, bread and frozen products will remain better available. CEO Margaret Versteden-van Duijn on the consequences for customers: "It is of course extremely annoying for customers when they go to a store and see that something is not available", says the top executive. Varies per store The supermarket chain does not yet know how long this situation will last. "Of course shelves will empty if it lasts longer. That will vary per store. It depends on a lot of factors", says the top executive. Albert Heijn cannot yet say whether malicious actors have broken into the company's IT systems. "The investigation is ongoing. Unfortunately I cannot say anything about that right now", said Versteden-van Duijn. The incident began yesterday afternoon. Earlier today Albert Heijn said it had shut down systems to protect the company's IT environment. These are photos taken at the end of the afternoon at AH stores in Utrecht and Zaandam: Because systems have been taken offline, customers in the store still see last week's promotional prices. They cannot see this week's discount offers. Albert Heijn says that nationwide bonus offers will still be applied at the checkout. Personal discounts linked to the Bonus card and the app are not working. "Customers who miss out on personal discounts as a result will be compensated as soon as possible", says Albert Heijn. "We ask customers to keep their receipts carefully for this." The savings systems are also not working. As a result, customers currently do not receive stamps in their Albert Heijn app when they make purchases. Offline during delivery When the problems started yesterday, many drivers delivering online orders were still on the road. "We use an online app to view the addresses and the schedule", a driver tells NOS. "You have to log in there with a personal account. Yesterday all drivers were suddenly kicked out of the app. Logging in has not worked since." Supermarkets in France experienced a cyberattack today, which caused the temperature of cooling systems to rise to 50 degrees. The top executive of Albert Heijn could not say whether the security incident at Albert Heijn has anything to do with this. A spokesperson for parent company Ahold Delhaize later told news agency Reuters that there is no reason to see a link between the two incidents.

title: New arrests for fatal shooting incident at Vierdaagsefeesten Nijmegen
lead: The <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> has arrested two new suspects in the investigation into the fatal shooting during the Vierdaagsefeesten in Nijmegen. They are a 19-year-old man from Amsterdam and a 21-year-old man from Hoorn. On Tuesday 21 July, at around 22.00 hours, an 18-year-old man from Rotterdam was shot dead on Graafseweg. This happened not far from the Vierdaagsefeesten, which were underway in the city at that moment. That same evening, an 18-year-old fellow city resident was arrested. He was released again a day later and has not been a suspect since, reports Omroep Gelderland . The police have since investigated the shooting incident and what preceded it. "This has now resulted in two arrests", the police report. The men are suspected of involvement in the shooting incident. The motive for the shooting is still being investigated. The police therefore are not currently sharing any further information about what the two are specifically suspected of.

title: Dead and injured in explosion in Israel from unexploded ordnance
lead: An explosion in northern Israel has left one person dead and 24 others injured. Among the victims are pupils and teachers from a secondary school, Israeli media report. The explosion took place near the kibbutz Yiftach, close to the border with Lebanon. According to Israeli media, the pupils were hiking in the area. According to a preliminary police investigation, the explosion was caused by unexploded ordnance. A pupil reportedly found an explosive during the hike and put it in his bag. According to the Israeli army, the explosive comes from a rocket fired at Israel by the Lebanese militant group Hezbollah. Three victims are seriously injured, Israeli media report. Israeli authorities are searching the area for more unexploded ordnance.

title: Raid on Congress member Ilhan Omar, an outspoken critic of Trump
lead: US authorities have raided the home of Democratic Congress member Ilhan Omar. The Justice Department has not yet said why the search took place, but sources tell Fox News that an investigation is being carried out into how she entered the country as a child from Somalia. As a progressive politician from the state of Minnesota, Omar is known as an outspoken critic of Trump. He has in the past accused her of fraud and spread internet rumours that she once married her brother. Omar spoke of intimidation after agents of Homeland Security searched her home in the capital Washington, but also said she would not let herself be "silenced" by Trump. In the past she already said the president has an "unhealthy and rancid obsession" with her. 'Abuse of power' The raid comes three weeks before important midterm elections in the US, in which Omar is also up for re-election. Trump's Republicans threaten to receive a heavy punishment there, due to the unpopular war he started in the Middle East and the high fuel prices that result from it. Democratic party colleagues condemn the raid on Omar and speak of abuse of power. "The government is being used against Donald Trump's opponents," says caucus leader Jeffries. "His violent mass deportation machine is now being used against a lawfully elected Congress member and her family." The Squad Ilhan Omar was born in Somalia in 1982 and was granted asylum in the US in 1995 with her family. When she was elected to Congress in 2019, she and Rashida Tlaib were the first Muslim women in the House of Representatives. Together they made a name for themselves as members of The Squad, a group of newly elected women who worked together in their fight for progressive policy. This led to Donald Trump attacking them regularly. For example, he called Omar and Tlaib "garbage" that had better "go back to where they come from" because they were "just complaining". Tlaib was born in Michigan. In general, Trump said this year that Somalis, who form an important minority in Minnesota, are "damn dishonest". In doing so he named Ilhan Omar by name. 'Jihadist lunatic' Trump recently also expressed himself in harsh terms about Omar's party colleague Abdul El-Sayed, who hopes to become senator for Michigan. Trump called him a radical extremist, a terror sympathiser and a "jihadist lunatic who hates our country". A spokesperson for Omar called the attacks on her earlier ridiculous lies, "aimed at distracting from an unpopular war that a party that protects paedophiles has opted for". Trump has in the past directed the Justice Department at individuals he regards as opponents. For example, in a public post he once asked his attorney general why there were still no cases against former FBI director Comey, Congress member Schiff and prosecutor James, who prosecuted him for fraud. According to The Wall Street Journal, that post was accidentally sent publicly and should have been a private message.

title: Riyad airport remains closed longer, KLM suspends more flights
lead: The international airport of Riyad, in Saudi Arabia, will remain closed until Saturday evening. This follows continued attacks by the Houthis from Yemen. Airlines have cancelled their flights. The airport will certainly remain closed until and including Saturday evening at 23.00 Dutch time. The airport was closed after the most serious attack in Saudi Arabia in ten years. Last Saturday thirteen people were killed and more than three hundred were injured. The airport was also targeted by an attack yesterday, in which another person died. The Saudi civil aviation authority reports that the airport will remain closed to "complete procedures that must ensure the safety and operational readiness of the airport facilities". The attacks by the Houthis are causing extra tension in the Middle East. Five questions and answers about this: The aviation sector has long been affected by conflicts in the Middle East. Because of attacks between the United States, Iran and Israel, several airports were closed a few months ago. In addition, fuel prices for aviation are rising. KLM KLM announced today that it is extending the suspension of flights to Saudi Arabia. The airline will not fly to Riyad and Dammam until and including 31 October at the least. In addition to the attacks on the international airport in Riyad, there was also an attack on Dammam, an important port city. The plan was to resume flights from 25 October, but that date has been postponed. KLM reports that affected passengers have been informed. They can rebook their flight or request a refund.

title: Minister Hermans scraps 13-week scan for pregnant women from 2028
lead: Pregnant women will no longer be able to use a 13-week scan from 1 January 2028. The current experiment with the scan to detect congenital abnormalities will not be continued, Minister Hermans of Health writes to <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity>. Last month the <entity id="org:gezondheidsraad">Gezondheidsraad</entity> advised against introducing the 13-week scan as a standard part of maternity care. The results of the scan did not always turn out to be correct; sometimes women were referred unnecessarily, while relatively many abnormalities were missed. The Gezondheidsraad concluded that the benefits do not currently outweigh the disadvantages. Hermans largely follows that advice, but goes one step further than the Gezondheidsraad. The council had still argued for further research to use the scan in such a way that the benefits would outweigh the disadvantages. But the minister is not keen on that. Unnecessary anxiety. "Although <entity id="org:kabinet">het kabinet</entity> takes the possibilities for improving the protocol seriously, there currently also appear to be many disadvantages to offering the 13-week scan again within a research setting", writes Hermans. She especially does not want to expose pregnant women again to unnecessary anxiety if the result turns out to be a false alarm. That means the 13-week scan will disappear on 1 January 2028. The research has been offered since 2021 as part of a scientific study, alongside the usual 20-week scan. The idea behind it was that parents with a scan in the thirteenth week of pregnancy have more time to prepare for a child who needs a lot of care or for a possible abortion. In her letter to the House, Hermans writes that she does want to examine the entire chain of prenatal screening. In doing so, she wants to look at how the current system, with scans and the NIPT blood test to detect genetic abnormalities, can be improved. If scientific developments give cause for it, she may ask the Gezondheidsraad again for advice on the 13-week scan.

title: Highest NATO military officer wants to reassure with speech, but doubts about US role remain
lead: Projecting that the alliance stands ready in case of a Russian attack was what the American NATO Supreme Allied Commander Alexus Grynkewich hoped to achieve with his speech at the security summit in Warsaw. That message came across to politicians and experts, but in the corridors the talk still centred on that one question: can NATO count on America when it matters? Grynkewich used the speech to reassure the 1 billion inhabitants of NATO countries: there is no war on the horizon, and if an attack does come, there is a plan. The general said he hoped it would never come to that, but he also wanted everyone to know: "We got this". Yet afterwards little relief is noticeable. Grynkewich may be NATO's highest military officer, but he must also relate to his president, Donald Trump. On Friday Trump concluded an agreement on the supply of diesel with Russian President Putin. In Grynkewich's account, Putin was precisely the enemy. Trump is, in any case, a repeat offender when it comes to sowing doubt about American involvement in NATO. "The doubt that prevails in the alliance (will the Americans really be there for us?) has not been removed by this", reacts security expert Bob Deen, director of Insitituut Clingendael. "This general is a military professional, but ultimately he must follow the political orders of the American government in particular. You could naturally see the doubt in the room there." Grynkewich himself was later asked in a panel discussion about the apparent contradiction between his words and the diesel deal. He also sounded reassuring then: "I am here with Trump's permission, and no one needs to doubt the US commitment to NATO", was his answer. Will American soldiers also fight if Russia attacks, the moderator wanted to know. "Ultimately that is a political decision", but doubt really isn't necessary, Grynkewich vowed. "I mean: I am here." The speech was at the same time tough. Grynkewich said he has no indications that an attack is imminent, but in clear language he already explained what NATO does in such a case: block the enemy, weaken it and ultimately break it. No one should think that NATO shies away from military action, he said. "And we will win." "This American four-star general, who was appointed by Trump, essentially said: we stand for Article 5 ('an attack on one is an attack on all')", reacts former top military officer Rob Bauer in Warsaw. "We will go all the way if necessary, was the message." 'Powerful and clear' That is also the takeaway for Defence Minister Yesilgöz, who was also present. She calls the speech powerful and clear. She does not see a contradiction between the words of the American president and those of the American NATO Supreme Allied Commander, although she acknowledges that "sometimes things happen that seem to clash". "President Zelensky of Ukraine was also here this morning", says Yesilgöz. "He emphasised: please make sure the deal between the US and Russia ensures that our energy supplies are left alone. I think we can better focus on that." Bauer also does not want to dwell too long on the question of what Grynkewich's words are worth. "Who are we actually helping by asking that question?" he asked rhetorically. He gave the answer himself: Putin. And Russia? Grynkewich used his speech to reassure the population in NATO countries. According to him, the intelligence apparatus would see immediately if Russia were preparing an attack. The most important thing, according to him, is deterring the enemy. He did not name Russia, but everyone knows who he meant. In Moscow they will undoubtedly have watched with interest. "This will be explained in Russia as an aggressive speech", Bauer expects. He thinks they will focus mainly on the announcement that enemies will be dealt with harshly. "They will use that internally to be able to mobilise for the war in Ukraine." Russia has difficulty gathering enough soldiers for that. Clingendael director Deen also thinks Putin has paid close attention. "The aim was mainly to make clear to Russia that there is no point in attacking NATO. That every attack will be stopped and ultimately broken." The Russian president will probably not have become truly worried, Deen says. "The main question he will have is: does it all add up? Is that unity in the alliance really that strong? He will keep testing that in the coming months."

title: British PM: Iranian Revolutionary Guard behind incident at air base
lead: Iran is "most likely" behind the suspicious situation at an air force base in the United Kingdom at the end of last month, Prime Minister Burnham tells Parliament. According to him, it was "almost certainly" directed by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard in Iran (IRG). Burnham stresses that the UK will impose further sanctions on Iran. The US and other allies have also condemned Iran's attacks and say they will act against anyone acting on behalf of Tehran. Last month a major alarm was raised over a security incident at the air base in Fairford, after white vans were seen in the vicinity. The counter-terrorism unit of the British police investigated, as there were fears that explosives were in the vans. Dozens of homes in the area were evacuated. The explosives unit ultimately found only cans of petrol in the vans. Five men were arrested that same day on suspicion of preparing a terrorist attack. Later, two more people were detained. All suspects have been released under conditions. A large number of American military personnel are stationed at the base. The base has been used by the Americans for bombing flights on Iran. The IRG said in July that any base involved in the war is considered a legitimate target. Ambassador summoned. The British Foreign Secretary, Miliband, has summoned the Iranian ambassador to make clear that "Britain will not tolerate threats on its own soil", writes the BBC. He calls Iran's "persistent attempts" to undermine the UK's security "unacceptable". The minister has also imposed sanctions on two Iranians, including the head of the country's counter-intelligence operations. The men have an entry ban and their assets have been frozen. Iran denies involvement.

title: Rail staff talk about suicide: 'standing talking to her for 1,5 hours'
lead: Start the conversation: that is the message of a new campaign for suicide prevention on the railways. Each year around 200 people die in the Netherlands in a collision with a train. Attempted suicides are far more common still. Train drivers, conductors and ProRail employees are now speaking out with their stories in a campaign by 113 and the railway companies. In this way they hope to contribute to reducing the number of suicides. NS head conductor Glenda (41) "I have now been head conductor for 8,5 years. In that period I have experienced one suicide and found perhaps twenty suicidal people. On the tracks, around the station, on the platform. Sometimes it happens very often in a row, sometimes not at all for a year. The first time I experienced it, we received an emergency call 'suicidal person'. After we had stood still for twenty minutes, we got permission to drive again. We were about two kilometres on our way when the driver paged me: 'There is someone in front of my train, can you come forward?' The driver said: 'She is a very young girl, maybe it is better if you go outside.' I then climbed out of the train. She was standing right in front of the train, with her arms wide, and shouted very loudly: 'Make sure he drives, make sure he drives.' I talked to her for about an hour and a half. Eventually she climbed into the train, we drove on and handed her over to the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity>. I have learned to recognise behaviour that is not understood, for example when it is very cold outside and someone is standing there in a T-shirt. I also now know how to deal with it. Do ask that direct question about suicide. If you are off the mark, someone will understand that it was asked with the best intentions. During rush hour I once saw a person standing completely still. Everyone walked around them. Something in me said: this is not right. I went over to them and took them out of the crowd. I did not go into their world until I asked: 'Are you here because you wanted to jump in front of the train?' Then I pulled her out of that daze and she said: 'Yes, that is what I came here to do.'" Incident responder at ProRail Dennis Heijne (34) "We are alerted to animals on the tracks, but also to people with behaviour that is not understood. When there is a collision we receive an alert. As team leader I then select the men and women who make sure the passengers of NS or Arriva can continue as quickly as possible. The number of collisions I have experienced is already getting close to 190. I always find the number a bit confronting to mention. And we have not even got to near-collisions or people around the tracks. You have to be able to deal with that, be able to hold conversations. Otherwise you cannot do this job. We are retrained several times a year. How can you share things? How do you talk about 'I'? It also happens several times a day that we prevent suicides. Then we can make sure people get the right help, if it has not yet been started. It may be that someone with behaviour that is not understood is seen on ProRail cameras, or by bystanders. We then go looking straight away, together with the police. To start a conversation, I first say who I am: Dennis from ProRail. Then I look for something to talk about, which can be something simple: 'I see you have an iPhone.' I want to make a connection, to get someone out of the danger zone. To a bench, away from that level crossing." 113 Are you thinking about suicide or worried about someone? Talking about it helps and can be done anonymously via the chat on www.113.nl or by phone on 113 or 0800-0113.

title: EU countries hold off on a hard response after US sanctions against the Court
lead: The European Union is for now choosing the diplomatic route to keep the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague standing. Harsh measures against the American sanctions against the court are not coming for now. That is the outcome of a meeting of the ministers of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-buitenlandse-zaken">Buitenlandse Zaken</entity> of the EU countries in Luxembourg. "The most important thing is to engage in dialogue and do everything to protect the court," said <entity id="person:tom-berendsen">minister Berendsen</entity> of Buitenlandse Zaken after the meeting. Belgium would have preferred to take a harder stance against the American sanctions, but does not get sufficient support. Last Friday the American government announced sanctions against the Court. The US is an opponent of the ICC. It does not recognise the court and demands that the ICC not prosecute American nationals. The arrest warrant against Israeli prime minister Netanyahu also led to great anger among Americans. After the sanctions take effect next April, it will be prohibited for American citizens, companies and organisations to do business with the ICC. Organisations outside the US also face sanctions if they cooperate with the court. Earlier, sanctions were already imposed on individual judges and prosecutors at the International Criminal Court. Unacceptable The EU countries called the sanctions unacceptable on Friday. They did stress, however, that the six-month period before the sanctions take effect still offers the chance to engage in talks with the United States. Belgium called today for doing more than just talking by now instructing companies to ignore the American sanctions. European rules offer that possibility. The Netherlands, like the majority of EU countries, wants to keep that option in reserve, partly out of fear that the conflict with the Americans over the Court will otherwise escalate, with possibly major financial consequences for companies. According to Belgian minister Prevot, a firm signal is precisely needed because some companies that now work with the Court are "preventively withdrawing their support." Minister Berendsen could not confirm that this is actually happening. He does see that there are concerns among companies. He therefore finds it important to engage in talks with companies, and to show "that they have full support to continue their work for the court". Red line? In the coming months it will become clear what negotiations will yield. The Americans want the court to no longer be able to prosecute American nationals. Experts stress that such a concession would jeopardise the functioning of the court. "If you grant immunity to residents of one country for the most serious international crimes, then you not only undermine the functioning of the court, but the entire international legal order," said professor of International criminal law Marieke de Hoon on Friday to Nieuwsuur. According to minister Berendsen, the independent functioning of the court is of crucial importance. Whether the American demand is therefore a red line he does not want to say, however: "It is not up to the Netherlands to determine what we can and cannot grant. That is up to the more than 120 countries that are affiliated with the Court". Greenland deal The hope is to still be able to convince the Americans in the coming months to lift the sanctions, without the functioning of the court suffering as a result. In Brussels the Greenland deal is mentioned as an example of how the Americans could still come round. Meanwhile, preparations are also continuing in case the Americans do actually impose the sanctions. In the coming months the countries that participate in the International Criminal Court will use the ICC to protect it as much as possible against the sanctions. They want to do this, among other things, by working with companies and banks that have no ties to the US at all. At an EU summit later this week in Brussels, the heads of government of the member states will also discuss the American sanctions with each other.

title: Ukraine now targets Russian data centres and the troll army
lead: The focus of the war between Russia and Ukraine is shifting from the oil industry to data centres. In recent days Ukrainian drones hit several locations of Yandex, often described as Russia's Google. The consequences are clearly felt in Russian society and on social media worldwide. On Thursday a centre in the Ryazan region went completely offline. A day later the location of the tech giant in Kaluga was partly rendered unusable. Yesterday Ukraine managed to hit the data centre in Vladimir, 175 kilometres east of Moscow. The attacks affect users in dozens of Russian cities, but also in neighbouring countries Kazakhstan, Belarus and Armenia. Residents of Moscow who want to use taxis, shared scooters, shared bicycles and meal deliveries are faced with error messages. Also, people cannot access their bank accounts, planning routes via the app is impossible, or they suffer from slow internet. Pavel Beljavski, a driver for Yandex Taxi, says it was unclear whether ride requests were coming in. He had to cancel several rides after long waits, because he could not get in touch with the passenger. "I pressed the call button to make contact, but nothing happened", he told news agency AP. "I couldn't do anything, so I was forced to cancel." Igor Mann failed to view the status of an order on the Yandex Market shopping platform. The page was unreachable, even via a VPN connection. "Nothing worked", he says. Troll army According to President Zelensky, the consequences of the attacks on the data centres are also being felt in the rest of the world. Online there are far fewer anti-Ukrainian bots active, he claims. He refers to computer programs that try to influence public opinion via fake accounts on social media. According to Zelensky, many people have noticed that on social media "less hatred, less division and fewer provocations" can be seen. In a video link at a security conference in Warsaw he said that "it is quite clear where those bots come from". Western governments have long accused Russia of spreading fake news and propaganda via countless fake user profiles. Yandex states that it is gradually restoring the company's services. It is unclear which parts that would apply to.

title: Musk quietly pours hundreds of millions into US midterm elections
lead: 366 million dollars. That is the amount Elon Musk has already put into the US midterm elections in November. With this he has already surpassed the total amount of his contribution to Trump's victory two years ago, but this time he is opting for a quiet approach. The New York Times gained access to the donations Musk has made this year to political candidates. The lion's share of 158 million went to the Senate Leadership Fund, the fund that supports Republican Senate candidates. Another 76 million he gave to his own America PAC, a political organization that itself campaigns for the party for some forty crucial Congress seats. He also put 10 million dollars into a campaign organization that supports Republican Ken Paxton in Musk's home state of Texas. That state is behind Democrat Talarico in the polls, notable for a right-wing candidate in the conservative state. In addition, Musk donated an unknown sum of money in the seven figures to various candidates. He did so in a way that does not have to be reported under the law. No more handing out cheques Musk also gave 290 million to Trump's campaign in the 2024 presidential election. His strategy is different this time, The New York Times notes. Where he previously opted for large campaign rallies where he controversially handed out cheques of one million to voters in swing states, now he mostly stays in the background. The paper also noticed that, unlike the previous election year, he is largely silent about the midterms on his busy X account. This year only four posts went out about candidates in key races. Under the spotlight Musk's spending is welcome in a year in which Republican candidates are under fire due to President Trump's unpopular policies, such as high fuel prices caused by the war with Iran. The money is not only used to advertise heavily for candidates, but also to personally recruit votes among conservative voters: this weekend 3000 canvassers paid by Musk were out and about. Musk's millions thus give the Republicans a considerable lead in fundraising: his contribution alone is already more than all the Democratic donors combined. A spokesperson for that party therefore says that Musk wants to buy the elections for the Republicans despite "unpopular candidates, an unpopular president and an unpopular economy". Musk is the richest man on earth, with a fortune fluctuating around a trillion dollars. If the Republicans lose their majority in Congress, Musk can count on the Democrats scrutinising his activities. For example, he has lucrative contracts with the US government for his companies such as SpaceX, and he had a controversial role in the radical cutting back of the US government.

title: Other (online) supermarkets are busier due to problems at Albert Heijn
lead: Due to the problems at Albert Heijn, other supermarket chains are busier. A spokesperson for Jumbo says that chain is already scaling up. Jumbo already sees an increase in online orders. The company cannot yet say whether more people are also coming to the stores because shelves are empty at some Albert Heijn branches. "We have to anticipate higher demand. If this lasts longer at Albert Heijn, there will definitely be a gap, of course. That is what we at Jumbo are trying to fill as well as possible." Jumbo says it is also in contact with the CBL, the trade organisation for supermarkets, about the situation. The chain wishes Albert Heijn much strength. "It is really tough for them", the spokesperson said. Stepping in: At online supermarket Picnic too, more is being ordered. "Since this morning we have seen an increase in the number of orders for tomorrow", says a spokesperson. "If it continues like this, we will end up with a few thousand extra orders, which is why we are currently scaling up our delivery capacity." Picnic says it hopes for Albert Heijn that the problems will be resolved quickly. "But if necessary, we can step in over the coming days." Trade organisation CBL says it is certainly thinking about what to do if Albert Heijn branches cannot be supplied for a longer period. "We are keeping an eye on it and of course we are thinking about it, but it is still a little early", says a spokesperson. "The Netherlands has a supermarket landscape that can absorb quite a bit. Our call is: just do your shopping as you normally would, there is no reason for panic." Customers at an Albert Heijn branch in Zaandam saw many empty shelves in the store: Albert Heijn is by far the largest supermarket chain in the Netherlands, with a market share last year of around 38 percent, according to research agency NielsenIQ. Jumbo follows with around 20 percent. The share of Albert Heijn parent company Ahold Delhaize fell today on the Amsterdam stock exchange by 2.8 percent, while the AEX index rose by about 0.4 percent. The ministry of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-landbouw-visserij-voedselzekerheid-en-natuur">Landbouw, Visserij, Voedselzekerheid en Natuur</entity> says the situation is worrying. "The problems underline the importance of a stronger and more resilient food system. It is good that Ahold's stores are open and that hard work is being done on a solution. The ministry is closely monitoring the situation and is in contact." Incident: Albert Heijn itself took all kinds of IT systems offline yesterday afternoon due to a 'cybersecurity incident'. Since then the website has not been working, you cannot order online, and several distribution centres of the chain are at a standstill. As a result, stores can be supplied less well and empty shelves are appearing here and there. What exactly is going on, and whether malicious actors have broken into Albert Heijn's systems, is still unclear.

title: End looms for Seal Centre as costly new building and setbacks deliver the final blow
lead: The Pieterburen Seal Centre, which recently moved into the Wadden Sea World Heritage Centre, is threatening to go bankrupt within two weeks. The centre has been struggling with financial problems for some time. These worsened further last week and now the end is really near, says the board. The immediate reason for the announcement is the loss of financial support that had been counted on. The centre says talks about that support were held with the municipality <entity id="org:gemeente-het-hogeland">Het Hogeland</entity>, which Lauwersoog falls under, and the <entity id="org:provincie-groningen">provincie Groningen</entity>. On Thursday they indicated they see no role for themselves, according to a statement from the centre. "We are shocked and saddened." If the centre does go bankrupt, forty people will lose their jobs. The care of sick and orphaned seals would also stop. Seal Centre and Wadden Sea World Heritage Centre The Pieterburen Seal Centre moved into the new Wadden Sea World Heritage Centre in Lauwersoog last year. Along with the Seal Centre, an interactive exhibition and research facilities are based there. The Seal Centre moved to the new location at the beginning of last year. The new building turned out more expensive than expected, and there were several setbacks. Not all bills have been paid yet. At the same time, income is falling short. This consists of donations and entrance tickets. Reserves are depleted, so the deficit keeps growing. It now stands at nearly 3 million euros. "There is still a small hope of a miracle to bridge this amount," says the centre. The board also admits its own part: "In hindsight we may have been too optimistic about visitor development and about addressing setbacks in time." Started out as a crèche The Pieterburen Seal Centre was founded in 1971. It became known as the Zeehondencrèche; most of the animals taken in there were orphaned young seals. From 2006 to 2014 the centre bore the name of its founder, Lenie 't Hart. She stepped down as director in 2012. Two years later she left the centre entirely after a dispute over policy.

title: Singer Heino receives compensation from AfD over false voting endorsement
lead: The German party AfD must pay compensation of 7,500 euros to schlager singer Heino (87). A candidate of the radical right party had said at state elections that the singer would vote for him. "Heino votes for Felix on Sunday", candidate Felix Teichner from the state of Brandenburg posted on social media. He added that the Uckermark region would colour "blue, blue, blue", a reference to both the AfD party colour and Heino's hit Blau blüht der Enzian. Heino immediately made known that he had never issued a voting endorsement. "It is scandalous that I am made the face of a political party without permission," he responded. "This action is absolutely going too far for me." He added that everyone of any political persuasion is welcome at his concerts. Image damage Due to damage to his image, Heino initially demanded compensation of 250,000 euros. Although that was later already adjusted to 30,000 euros, he ultimately agreed to a settlement of 7,500 euros. Teichner had previously already removed the post and also offered apologies. With that, the matter is closed for Heino and his management. Incidentally, Teichner lost the election to a CDU candidate.

title: Major cyber incident at Albert Heijn: 'You don't just take measures like these lightly'
lead: Cybersecurity experts consider it very plausible that someone has broken into the systems of Albert Heijn. Since Sunday afternoon, the online systems of the supermarket chain have been taken offline as a precaution, which is causing major problems in the stores. Albert Heijn does not want to say whether there has been a hack and for now itself speaks of a digital security incident. "Such a large organisation does not just take major measures of this kind lightly," says cybersecurity expert Joey Fennis. "If malicious actors have turned the key in the front door lock, they have probably also looked inside and viewed or taken data." Fennis says that similar measures are taken when that happens. As a result of the outage, Albert Heijn's systems are unavailable, online orders cannot be delivered and some distribution centres are at a standstill, leaving stores with empty shelves. According to Fennis, the top of the company must give permission to take this kind of measure. "Apparently the concern is so great that it reminds me of the <entity id="org:openbaar-ministerie">Openbaar Ministerie</entity> last year." The OM was hacked at the time via a vulnerability in a program that employees use to work from home. 'Outages usually don't last that long' The fact that drastic action has been taken also leads cybersecurity expert Pim Takkenberg to suspect that there is more going on. "It seems quite clear that a malicious actor has been in the system. Albert Heijn has preventively shut down a number of systems, which is very common to prevent further damage when someone is in your systems," he says on Nieuwsuur. "An outage usually doesn't last that long." Customers at an Albert Heijn branch in Zaandam saw many empty shelves in the store: If a criminal group is behind the outage, according to Takkenberg they are usually after money. "They try to hack systems, steal data and then threaten to publish it if you don't pay. Perhaps a group will come forward later." According to him, it could be a state actor such as Russia, or so-called 'hacktivists' with some kind of ideological aim. But Takkenberg considers it most plausible that a criminal group is responsible. "I think there is no Russian state actor involved in the Netherlands, because all the signals I am seeing now are of a different order of magnitude, although I cannot rule it out. It seems unlikely to me that this belongs to a Russian state actor. This incident fits much more the pattern of criminal groups," said the cybersecurity expert. Fennis fears for customers' data, because those systems have also gone offline. "Just like with Flink, they may be after personal data." An unknown group of hackers broke into that grocery delivery service. Customers were digitally extorted. According to cybersecurity expert Eward Driehuis, it may also be that Albert Heijn itself has found a vulnerability in its system. "If that is not easy to fix, they may be closing the digital doors as a precaution." "What does become clear is how dependent we are on IT and the cyber domain, including for people who do not work with it daily," says Driehuis. "That becomes very concrete now that you can't do your grocery shopping. It is, however, a good eye-opener for people." Because of the outage, Albert Heijn branches are increasingly running out of supplies. Throughout the day, photos came in of stores without stock; fresh products in particular are missing. Meanwhile, other supermarket chains are seeing an increase in orders. Number of days? According to Fennis, it cannot be said how long the problems will last. "That depends on whether they were in time. The question is how far any criminals have got and how long they have been able to carry on, but that is still speculation for now. The investigation will have to show that." "Albert Heijn only communicated about the outage this morning, even though it had been going on for some time. In the best case, I think it will take a number of days."

title: Smulders, Ostermann and Yentl en de Boer win cabaret prize Poelifinario
lead: Ruud Smulders, Lisa Ostermann and the duo Yentl en de Boer have won a Poelifinario, the most important Dutch cabaret prize. This took place during the Cabaret Gala at Theater Diligentia in The Hague. The Neerlands Hoop prize for promising theatre maker went to David Linszen. The prizes are awarded by the Vereniging van Schouwburg- en Concertgebouwdirecties (VSCD). Smulders won the prize in the Entertainment category. It was the first time he won the prize. Ostermann won in the Engagement category. It was her second Poelifinario. The jury praised her combination of "pure candour and delightfully nonsensical silliness". Bears on the road: The duo Yentl en de Boer also received a Poelifinario for the second time. They won in the Kleinkunst category. "Their distinctive humour gives free rein to crazy songs about bears on the road, promised presents you never had and the bizarre experience of a man being sung to on his deathbed", the jury said. At the gala there was also attention for the recently deceased cabaret performer and writer Paulien Cornelisse. For the award ceremony, the duo Yentl en de Boer sang a song for her.
